Fact.Name: Did you pay any one household employee cash wages of $2,800 or more in 2025?
Fact.Description:
Schedule H line A, verbatim: "Did you pay any one household employee cash wages of $2,800 or more in 2025? (If any household employee was your spouse, your child under age 21, your parent, or anyone under age 18, see the line A instructions before you answer this question.)" (https://www.irs.gov/pub/irs-pdf/f1040sh.pdf, page 1).
AN ATTESTATION, NOT A DERIVATION, and the parenthetical is why: the question is asked of ONE employee at a time ("any ONE household employee"), against a per-employee exclusion list that turns on relationship and age, with two further printed exceptions (a parent caring for the filer's own under-18 or disabled child in stated circumstances; an under-18 employee for whom household service is their principal occupation) - see https://www.irs.gov/pub/irs-pdf/i1040sh.pdf, page 4.
IT STAYS A WRITABLE EVEN THOUGH THE COLLECTION NOW MAKES IT DERIVABLE, and that is a decision rather than an omission. /householdEmployees carries the relationship and age facts, so /scheduleHHouseholdEmployeesSupportLineA computes this same question exactly; but line A is also the CHECKBOX whose being-asked-at-all /scheduleHGateIsComplete tests, and a derived line A would resolve Complete false for every return that never saw the section - which would silently neuter /knockoutHouseholdEmployeeWithoutScheduleHAnswers, the module's principal residual guard. So the printed box stays the filer's, and the collection is used to CHECK it: a Yes with no qualifying employee behind it is refused (arm 1 of /knockoutScheduleHRequiredButIncomplete).
EMPLOYEES WHOSE TAXES ARE REPORTED ELSEWHERE DO NOT COUNT. An employee whose employment taxes the filer reports on their business Form 941, 943 or 944, or that a section 3504 agent or a government agency reports and pays, is not reported on Schedule H (https://www.irs.gov/pub/irs-pdf/i1040sh.pdf, pages 2, 9, 10); neither is an F, J, M or Q nonimmigrant whose service is excluded from employment. A Yes resting only on such an employee is refused (/householdEmployees/*/writableTaxesReportedOnBusinessReturnOrByAgent, /householdEmployees/*/writableIsNonresidentAlienVisaPurposeService).
UNANSWERED IS THE NORMAL STATE. No intake asks this today (SERVICE-owned, invariant #7), so /scheduleHLineA resolves false and Part I computes to zero. The filer who HAS such an employee and is never asked is caught by /knockoutHouseholdEmployeeWithoutScheduleHAnswers, not by this fact.

Fact.Name: Schedule H line A, complete-safe
Fact.Description: The line A answer with unanswered read as No. Complete-safe by the standard All(IsComplete, value) alias so that a return which never sees the question resolves a Complete false rather than contaminating every downstream Schedule H line with Incompleteness.

Fact.Name: Did you withhold federal income tax during 2025 for any household employee?
Fact.Description:
Schedule H line B, verbatim: "Did you withhold federal income tax during 2025 for any household employee?" (https://www.irs.gov/pub/irs-pdf/f1040sh.pdf, page 1). Yes routes past line C straight to line 7.
AN ATTESTATION. Withholding from a household employee is optional and by agreement: "You're not required to withhold federal income tax from wages you pay a household employee. You should withhold federal income tax only if your household employee asks you to withhold it and you agree" (https://www.irs.gov/pub/irs-pdf/i1040sh.pdf, page 5), so nothing in the return implies the answer.
ONLY REACHED WHEN LINE A IS NO. A Yes on line A skips lines B and C outright, so this answer changes nothing on such a return: line 7 is already in play through Part I. The gating lives on /scheduleHLine7 and /scheduleHGateIsComplete, not here.

Fact.Name: Schedule H line B, complete-safe
Fact.Description: The line B answer with unanswered read as No, by the same All(IsComplete, value) alias as /scheduleHLineA.

Fact.Name: Did you pay total cash wages of $1,000 or more in any calendar quarter of 2024 or 2025?
Fact.Description:
Schedule H lines C AND 9 - one question, one writable. The printed text is identical in both places: "Did you pay total cash wages of $1,000 or more in any calendar quarter of 2024 or 2025 to all household employees? (Don't count cash wages paid in 2024 or 2025 to your spouse, your child under age 21, or your parent.)" (https://www.irs.gov/pub/irs-pdf/f1040sh.pdf, page 1 for line C, lines 53-54 for line 9). The two boxes exist only because the routing reaches the question by two different paths - line C for the filer who answered No to both A and B, line 9 for the filer who answered Yes to A or B - never both on the same return. Modelling them as ONE fact is not a simplification: it makes the two boxes incapable of disagreeing, which two independent writables with no consistency guard could not guarantee.
A PRIOR-YEAR ATTESTATION, AND FAITHFUL AS SUCH. The test reaches back into 2024 and this graph holds no prior-year state, but the printed form does not ask the graph - it asks the taxpayer about their own quarterly payroll records, exactly as line A asks about 2025. So an attestation IS the model, not a substitute for one. It is nonetheless uncheckable by construction: an understated answer skips Part II entirely and under-states FUTA, and nothing in the return can contradict it. Recorded here rather than papered over.
WHAT IT GATES: Part II (FUTA) in full, and, when A and B are both No, whether the return files a Schedule H at all ("No. Stop. Don't file this schedule.").

Fact.Name: Schedule H lines C and 9, complete-safe
Fact.Description: The $1,000-quarter answer with unanswered read as No. This is the FUTA gate: Part II is entered only on a Yes.

Fact.Name: Schedule H must be filed
Fact.Description:
"You must file Schedule H if you answer 'Yes' to any of the questions on lines A, B, and C of Schedule H" (https://www.irs.gov/pub/irs-pdf/i1040sh.pdf, page 2). Its complement is line C's own "No. Stop. Don't file this schedule." (https://www.irs.gov/pub/irs-pdf/f1040sh.pdf, page 1), reached only after No on A and No on B, so the two statements are the same rule read from opposite ends.
Note this fact says nothing about whether the questions were ASKED - all three arms are complete-safe to false, so an untouched return reads "not required". Whether the questions were asked is /scheduleHGateIsComplete, and the difference between the two is exactly the gap /knockoutHouseholdEmployeeWithoutScheduleHAnswers refuses.
EXPORTED rather than consumed inside this module: it is the "attach Schedule H" flag Schedule 2 line 9 names ("Household employment taxes. Attach Schedule H"), which is a filing-surface fact rather than an input to any dollar here. It deliberately does NOT gate /knockoutScheduleHRequiredButIncomplete, whose Part I completeness obligation must not reach the line-C filer who skips lines 1 through 9 altogether.

Fact.Name: The line A / B / C chain was actually walked
Fact.Description:
Whether the filer was asked, and answered, every gate question the printed routing puts in front of them. This is NOT "Schedule H is required" - it is "the question of whether Schedule H is required has been settled", which an untouched return has not.
THE ROUTING, EXACTLY AS PRINTED. Line A must always be answered. If line A is Yes the chain ends there ("Yes. Skip lines B and C and go to line 1"). If line A is No, line B must be answered; if line B is Yes the chain ends ("Yes. Skip line C and go to line 7"). If line B is also No, line C must be answered ("No. Go to line C"). Source: https://www.irs.gov/pub/irs-pdf/f1040sh.pdf, page 1.
WHY IT IS A FACT RATHER THAN A COMMENT: it is the predicate /knockoutHouseholdEmployeeWithoutScheduleHAnswers negates. A return that Form 2441 column (d) says has a household employee, and that has not walked this chain, would otherwise file a $0 Schedule H silently.

Fact.Name: How a household employee is related to the filer
Fact.Description:
The three relationships the printed exclusion lists name, plus everyone else. Line A: "To figure the total cash wages you paid in 2025 to each household employee, don't include amounts paid to any of the following individuals. Your spouse. Your child who was under age 21. Your parent. (See Exception for parents below.) Your employee who was under age 18 at any time during 2025" (https://www.irs.gov/pub/irs-pdf/i1040sh.pdf, page 4), and line 15's shorter list names the same first three (lines 362-371).
THE UNDER-18 TEST IS NOT A RELATIONSHIP and is carried separately on ../writableWasUnder18AtAnyTimeIn2025: it reaches ANY employee, related or not, and line 15 does not carry it at all. A CHILD AGED 21 OR OVER is `other`, which is what the printed "under age 21" qualifier means. The option set follows the printed lists rather than a general relationship taxonomy, so that each option maps to exactly one printed bullet.

Fact.Name: The filer's household employees, one row per employee
Fact.Description:
The per-employee collection Schedule H lines 1, 3, 5 and 15 are computed from. Every one of the four printed caps is PER EMPLOYEE - the $2,800 test, the $176,100 social security wage base, the $200,000 Additional Medicare Tax threshold and the $7,000 FUTA base - so a return-level total cannot be tested against any of them. This collection is what makes them derivable.
ONE ROW PER EMPLOYEE, NOT PER PAYMENT. Each printed cap is applied to "that employee's cash wages" for the year (https://www.irs.gov/pub/irs-pdf/i1040sh.pdf, pages 5-6), so the row's grain is the employee and its wage figure is the annual total.
WHO IS A HOUSEHOLD EMPLOYEE. "If you hired someone to do household work and you could control what work they did and how they did it, you had a household employee. This is true even if you gave the employee freedom of action. What matters is that you had the right to control the details of how the work was done" (https://www.irs.gov/pub/irs-pdf/i1040sh.pdf, page 2). Workers from an agency that is responsible for who does the work and how, and self-employed workers who alone control how the work is done, are not household employees (lines 108-115) and are not listed here. The control test is the filer's to apply when listing a row; no row field asks it again.
NO INTAKE ASKS IT TODAY (SERVICE-owned surface, invariant #7), which is why an empty collection is the normal state and every line below is complete-safe to zero. The completeness guards that keep a zero from becoming a silent filing live at /scheduleHPartIAnswersAreComplete and /scheduleHPartIIAnswersAreComplete.

Fact.Name: Cash wages paid to this employee in 2025
Fact.Description:
The employee's total 2025 cash wages, before any of the four printed caps. "Cash wages include wages paid by check, money order, etc. Cash wages don't include the value of food, lodging, clothing, transit passes, or other noncash items you give a household employee. However, cash you give your employee in place of these items is included in cash wages" (https://www.irs.gov/pub/irs-pdf/i1040sh.pdf, page 4).
THE UNCAPPED FIGURE, DELIBERATELY. Every cap this module applies is computed from this number rather than assumed to have been applied to it, which is the whole point of the collection: the filer states what they paid, the graph states what goes on each line. Sign: NON-NEGATIVE, carried as a declared Limit.
AN UNANSWERED WAGE FIGURE IS REFUSED, not defaulted - see ../rowIsIncomplete. A zero here would shrink all four lines and UNDER-state the tax, which is the direction this module refuses.

Fact.Name: This employee's relationship to the filer
Fact.Description:
Which printed exclusion bullet, if any, this employee falls under. See /householdEmployeeRelationshipOptions for the option set and why it mirrors the printed bullets.
AN UNANSWERED RELATIONSHIP IS NOT REFUSED. It resolves as `other`, which INCLUDES the employee in all four lines and therefore OVER-states the tax. The module refuses the under-stating direction only (/knockoutScheduleHRequiredButIncomplete), so this omission is left to cost the filer money rather than to stop their return.

Fact.Name: Was this employee under age 18 at any time during 2025?
Fact.Description:
The fourth line-A exclusion bullet: "Your employee who was under age 18 at any time during 2025. If the employee wasn't a student, see Exception for employees under age 18 below" (https://www.irs.gov/pub/irs-pdf/i1040sh.pdf, page 4).
LINES 1, 3 AND 5 ONLY. Line 15's exclusion list stops at the parent and carries no under-18 bullet (lines 362-371), so this fact must never reach ../line15Wages - the two lists are genuinely different and collapsing them is the trap this collection exists to avoid.
Unanswered resolves as No (the employee is included), which OVER-states and is therefore not refused.

Fact.Name: Was this under-18 employee a student?
Fact.Description:
The first half of the printed under-18 exception: "Include the cash wages you paid to a person who was under age 18 and not a student if providing household services was the employee's principal occupation" (https://www.irs.gov/pub/irs-pdf/i1040sh.pdf, page 4). A STUDENT UNDER 18 IS EXCLUDED WHATEVER THEIR OCCUPATION, because the printed exception requires "under age 18 AND NOT a student"; the occupation test is reached only after this one fails.
Asked only of an employee who was under 18 (../writableWasUnder18AtAnyTimeIn2025); an answer on any other row changes nothing.

Fact.Name: Was providing household services this employee's principal occupation?
Fact.Description:
The second half of the printed under-18 exception (see ../writableWasStudent for the quoted text, https://www.irs.gov/pub/irs-pdf/i1040sh.pdf, page 4). When it is Yes for a non-student under 18, the employee is INCLUDED in lines 1, 3 and 5 despite the age bullet.
AN UNANSWERED ANSWER ON A NON-STUDENT UNDER-18 ROW IS REFUSED (../rowIsIncomplete), because the default would exclude the employee and UNDER-state the tax.

Fact.Name: Parent exception test (1): did a child in the home need an adult's personal care?
Fact.Description:
Condition (1) of the printed two-part parent exception: "Include the cash wages you paid your parent for work in or around your home if both (1) and (2) below apply. 1. Your child (including an adopted child or stepchild) who lived with you was under age 18 or had a physical or mental condition that required the personal care of an adult for at least 4 continuous weeks during the calendar quarter in which services were performed" (https://www.irs.gov/pub/irs-pdf/i1040sh.pdf, page 4).
Asked only of a row whose relationship is `parent`. AN UNANSWERED ANSWER ON A PARENT ROW IS REFUSED (../rowIsIncomplete): the default excludes the parent and UNDER-states.

Fact.Name: Parent exception test (2): was the filer single, widowed, or living with a spouse unable to care for the child?
Fact.Description:
Condition (2) of the printed two-part parent exception: "You were divorced and not remarried, a widow or widower, or married to and living with a person whose physical or mental condition prevented your spouse from caring for the child for at least 4 continuous weeks during the calendar quarter in which services were performed" (https://www.irs.gov/pub/irs-pdf/i1040sh.pdf, page 4).
BOTH CONDITIONS MUST HOLD - the instruction prints "if both (1) and (2) below apply" - so this fact and ../writableParentExceptionChildNeededCare are conjoined at ../parentExceptionApplies rather than either one standing alone. Unanswered on a parent row is refused, for the reason given there.

Fact.Name: Which filer employed this household employee
Fact.Description:
The employer attribution the successor contract's obligation (c) asked for. "Only two Schedules H can be attached to Form 1040, 1040-SR, and 1040-SS, one Schedule H for each of the primary taxpayer and the secondary taxpayer" (https://www.irs.gov/pub/irs-pdf/i1040sh.pdf, page 4), so on an MFJ return each household employee belongs to one spouse's schedule, not to the return.
WHAT IT DOES. It carries the SIGNAL that a return has two household employers (/scheduleHReturnHasTwoHouseholdEmployers), which no fact in this graph held before it - Form 2441 column (d) identifies care providers, not which spouse employs them. IT ALSO MOVES MONEY: /filers/*/scheduleHLine20 sums only the employees THIS filer employed, so the attribution decides which schedule a wage lands on and therefore which 5.4% ceiling clips the credit against it. The successor contract that was "now buildable BECAUSE this fact exists" is filled; its line 17 counterpart is /scheduleHFutaStateContributions/*/writableEmployerFiler.
IT ALSO ACQUIRED A GUARD, WHICH IS NOW GONE AGAIN. While no dollar read this writable, a SINGLE return attributing an employee to a secondary filer was inert; from the per-filer landing it is a real mis-attribution, which was refused for two weeks and is now SCOPED instead: ../belongsOnThisReturn keeps such a row off a non-joint return's one printed schedule.
UNANSWERED IS THE PRIMARY FILER, which is exact for the single-employer majority the contract's obligation (c) warned against burdening: one employer means one schedule and the attribution question never needs to be asked.

Fact.Name: Cash reimbursements for qualified parking paid to this employee in 2025
Fact.Description:
The cash you paid this employee in 2025 to reimburse qualified parking, INCLUDED in ../writableCashWages. "If you reimburse your employee for qualified parking, transportation in a commuter highway vehicle, or transit passes, you may be able to exclude the cash reimbursement amounts from counting as cash wages subject to social security and Medicare taxes. Qualified parking is parking at or near your home or at or near a location from which your employee commutes to your home. It doesn't include parking at or near your employee's home. For 2025, you can reimburse your employee up to $325 per month for qualified parking ... Any cash reimbursement over these amounts is included as wages" (https://www.irs.gov/pub/irs-pdf/i1040sh.pdf, page 5).
HOW MUCH LEAVES THE WAGES. Enter only reimbursements that stayed within $325 for each month; the graph cannot see the months, so it caps the year at twelve months of $325 (../transportationReimbursementExclusion) and a monthly excess the filer entered here stays taxed only if the filer leaves it out. The amount leaves lines 1, 3 and 5 (IRC 3121(a)(20)) and line 15 (IRC 3306(b)(16), the FUTA twin the instruction does not repeat).
Unanswered is zero: the reimbursement stays in wages, which OVER-states and is not refused. An amount larger than the cash wages entered contradicts that entry and refuses the return (../rowIsIncomplete). Sign: NON-NEGATIVE.

Fact.Name: Cash reimbursements for commuter highway vehicle transportation and transit passes paid to this employee in 2025
Fact.Description: The cash you paid this employee in 2025 to reimburse transportation in a commuter highway vehicle and transit passes, INCLUDED in ../writableCashWages. The limit is "$325 per month for combined commuter highway vehicle transportation and transit passes", separate from the parking limit (https://www.irs.gov/pub/irs-pdf/i1040sh.pdf, page 5); see ../writableQualifiedParkingReimbursement for how the exclusion is applied. Transit passes you GIVE the employee (not cash) are noncash and are never in cash wages to begin with (lines 270-275), so they are not entered here. Sign: NON-NEGATIVE.

Fact.Name: Was this employee a nonresident alien in F, J, M or Q status working for the purpose of that status?
Fact.Description:
Whether the employee was a nonresident alien temporarily in the United States as an F, J, M or Q nonimmigrant and the household work was performed to carry out the purpose of that status (a J-1 au pair is the common case). Such service is not employment for social security and Medicare (IRC 3121(b)(19)) or for FUTA (IRC 3306(c)(19)), so the employee's wages reach none of lines 1, 3, 5 and 15 and do not count toward the $2,800 test. The printed instructions do not list this exclusion; the statute is clear and is followed.
Unanswered is No (the employee is included), which OVER-states and is not refused. A Yes together with line A answered Yes and no other qualifying employee is refused as a line A Yes with no employee behind it.

Fact.Name: Were this employee's wages covered only by a foreign country's social security system under a totalization agreement?
Fact.Description:
Whether a social security totalization agreement between the United States and another country makes this employee's wages subject exclusively to that country's system (the employer holds the foreign certificate of coverage). Such wages are exempt from the employee and employer social security and Medicare taxes (IRC 3101(c), IRC 3111(c)), so they reach none of lines 1, 3 and 5. FUTA has no totalization exemption, so they still reach line 15.
Unanswered is No (the employee is included), which OVER-states and is not refused.

Fact.Name: Are this employee's employment taxes reported on your business employment tax returns or by an agent or government agency?
Fact.Description:
Whether this employee's social security, Medicare, withheld income and FUTA taxes are reported somewhere other than Schedule H: on the Form 941, 943 or 944 (with Form 940) the filer files for their business employees, or by a section 3504 agent or a government agency paying them on the filer's behalf. "Don't use Schedule H if you chose to report employment taxes for your household employees along with your other employees on Form 941 or 941 (sp), Employer's QUARTERLY Federal Tax Return; Form 943 ... or Form 944" (https://www.irs.gov/pub/irs-pdf/i1040sh.pdf, page 10, continued at 597-601) and "If a government agency or third-party agent reports and pays the employment taxes on wages paid to your household employee on your behalf, you don't need to file Schedule H to report those taxes" (lines 97-106). A Yes takes the employee off lines 1, 3, 5 and 15 so the taxes are not assessed a second time; federal income tax withheld from such an employee stays off line 7 for the same reason.
Unanswered is No (the employee is included), which OVER-states and is not refused.

Fact.Name: This employee's cash wages, complete-safe
Fact.Description: ../writableCashWages with unanswered read as zero, so that a half-finished collection does not contaminate every Schedule H line with Incompleteness. The zero is SAFE ONLY BECAUSE ../rowIsIncomplete refuses the row that produced it: on its own a zero here under-states, and the refusal is what makes the complete-safe alias honest rather than convenient.

Fact.Name: This employee's qualified transportation reimbursements that leave wages
Fact.Description: The two reimbursement amounts, each floored at zero and capped at twelve months of the $325 monthly limit, added: "up to $325 per month for qualified parking and $325 per month for combined commuter highway vehicle transportation and transit passes ... Any cash reimbursement over these amounts is included as wages" (https://www.irs.gov/pub/irs-pdf/i1040sh.pdf, page 5). Unanswered amounts are zero.

Fact.Name: This employee's cash wages after the transportation exclusion
Fact.Description: ../cashWages less ../transportationReimbursementExclusion, floored at zero: the cash wages that count toward the $2,800 test and enter lines 1, 3, 5 and 15. The reimbursements are excluded "from counting as cash wages subject to social security and Medicare taxes" (https://www.irs.gov/pub/irs-pdf/i1040sh.pdf, page 5), and the FUTA definition of wages excludes the same benefit (IRC 3306(b)(16)). The floor never binds on a consistent row: an exclusion larger than the cash wages refuses the return (../rowIsIncomplete).

Fact.Name: This employee's service is F, J, M or Q nonimmigrant service, complete-safe
Fact.Description: ../writableIsNonresidentAlienVisaPurposeService with unanswered read as No.

Fact.Name: This employee's wages are covered by a totalization agreement, complete-safe
Fact.Description: ../writableIsCoveredByTotalizationAgreement with unanswered read as No.

Fact.Name: This employee's taxes are reported outside Schedule H, complete-safe
Fact.Description: ../writableTaxesReportedOnBusinessReturnOrByAgent with unanswered read as No.

Fact.Name: This employee is the filer's spouse
Fact.Description: The first bullet on BOTH printed exclusion lists - line A's (https://www.irs.gov/pub/irs-pdf/i1040sh.pdf, page 4) and line 15's (line 368) - and the only one that carries no exception on either list. Complete-safe to false on an unanswered relationship, which includes the employee and over-states; see ../writableRelationship for the direction argument.

Fact.Name: This employee is the filer's child under age 21
Fact.Description: The second bullet on both printed exclusion lists, "Your child who was under age 21" (https://www.irs.gov/pub/irs-pdf/i1040sh.pdf, pages 4, 6). A child aged 21 or over is `other` and is not excluded by either list; the age is inside the option rather than a separate fact because the printed bullet is written that way.

Fact.Name: This employee is the filer's parent
Fact.Description: The third bullet on both printed exclusion lists. THE TWO LISTS TREAT IT DIFFERENTLY, which is exactly why this fact is separate from ../isSpouse and ../isChildUnder21: line A prints "Your parent. (See Exception for parents below.)" (https://www.irs.gov/pub/irs-pdf/i1040sh.pdf, page 4) while line 15 prints a bare "Your parent." with no exception at all (line 370). So a parent can be INCLUDED in lines 1, 3 and 5 and still EXCLUDED from line 15.

Fact.Name: The printed parent exception applies to this employee
Fact.Description:
Both numbered conditions of "Exception for parents" hold for a row whose relationship is `parent`: "Include the cash wages you paid your parent for work in or around your home if both (1) and (2) below apply" (https://www.irs.gov/pub/irs-pdf/i1040sh.pdf, page 4). When it is true the parent is INCLUDED in lines 1, 3 and 5.
IT NEVER REACHES LINE 15. Line 15's list carries no exception, so ../isExcludedFromFutaWages does not read this fact.

Fact.Name: The under-18 bullet excludes this employee from lines 1, 3 and 5
Fact.Description:
The employee was under 18 at some point in 2025 AND the printed exception does not rescue them. The exception is "under age 18 and not a student if providing household services was the employee's principal occupation" (https://www.irs.gov/pub/irs-pdf/i1040sh.pdf, page 4), so it rescues only a NON-STUDENT whose principal occupation was household services; a student under 18 is excluded whatever their occupation.
LINES 1, 3 AND 5 ONLY - line 15's list has no under-18 bullet.

Fact.Name: This employee is off the line A / lines 1, 3 and 5 list
Fact.Description:
The FOUR-bullet printed list, with both of its exceptions applied: spouse, child under 21, parent (unless ../parentExceptionApplies), and an employee under 18 (unless the principal-occupation exception rescues them, ../under18ExclusionApplies) (https://www.irs.gov/pub/irs-pdf/i1040sh.pdf, page 4). Three further exclusions the printed list does not carry: F, J, M or Q nonimmigrant service performed for the purpose of that status (IRC 3121(b)(19)), wages a totalization agreement leaves only to a foreign system (IRC 3101(c), 3111(c)), and an employee whose taxes a business employment tax return or a section 3504 agent reports (https://www.irs.gov/pub/irs-pdf/i1040sh.pdf, pages 2, 10).
NOT THE SAME LIST AS LINE 15's, which is the trap this collection exists to avoid: see ../isExcludedFromFutaWages, which is three bullets and no exceptions.

Fact.Name: This employee is off the line 15 list
Fact.Description:
THREE bullets and NO exceptions: "don't include cash wages paid in 2025 to any of the following individuals. Your spouse. Your child who was under age 21. Your parent." (https://www.irs.gov/pub/irs-pdf/i1040sh.pdf, page 6). Two further exclusions the printed list does not carry: F, J, M or Q nonimmigrant service (IRC 3306(c)(19)) and an employee whose taxes a business employment tax return or a section 3504 agent reports. A totalization agreement does not reach FUTA, so it is NOT on this list. The printed list stops there - no under-18 bullet, and no parent exception - so a parent is excluded here even when ../parentExceptionApplies puts them ON lines 1, 3 and 5, and a 16-year-old is included here even when the age bullet takes them off those lines.
THAT DIVERGENCE IS THE POINT. The successor contract named a single per-employee exclusion flag as the trap a careless fill would walk into, and these two facts are the answer: different lists, argued separately, from the two printed passages.

Fact.Name: This employee meets the printed $2,800 test
Fact.Description:
"$2,800 test. If you pay a household employee $2,800 or more in cash wages during 2025, you must report and pay social security and Medicare taxes on all the wages, including the first $2,800 paid to that employee. The test applies to cash wages paid in 2025 regardless of when the wages were earned" (https://www.irs.gov/pub/irs-pdf/i1040sh.pdf, page 5).
AT OR ABOVE, NOT ABOVE: the printed words are "$2,800 or more", so the boundary employee at exactly $2,800.00 IS counted and the one at $2,799.99 is not. ALL THE WAGES, NOT THE EXCESS. Once the test is met the whole figure enters lines 1 and 3 - "including the first $2,800" - which is why ../line1Wages and ../line3Wages carry no subtraction.

Fact.Name: This employee's wages reach lines 1, 3 and 5
Fact.Description:
Not excluded by line A's list AND meeting the $2,800 test - the two printed gates lines 1 and 3 share ("Enter the total of cash wages ... paid in 2025 to each household employee who meets the $2,800 test", https://www.irs.gov/pub/irs-pdf/i1040sh.pdf, page 5; line 3 repeats it at lines 315-318).
LINE 5 SHARES THE SAME EMPLOYEE SET, and that is a printed statement rather than an extension of the $2,800 test to a line that does not name it: "All wages that are subject to Medicare tax are subject to Additional Medicare Tax withholding if paid in excess of the $200,000 withholding threshold" (lines 291-293). Line 3's set IS the wages subject to Medicare tax, so line 5 is drawn from it and the $2,800 test binds vacuously there - no employee paid over $200,000 can fail it.

Fact.Name: This employee's contribution to Schedule H line 1
Fact.Description:
The employee's cash wages capped at the social security wage base: "If you paid any household employee cash wages of more than $176,100 in 2025, include on line 1 only the first $176,100 of that employee's cash wages" (https://www.irs.gov/pub/irs-pdf/i1040sh.pdf, page 5). Zero for an employee who does not reach lines 1, 3 and 5 (../countsForSocialSecurityAndMedicare).
THE CAP IS PER EMPLOYEE, which is the whole reason this fact lives on the row rather than on the return: capping a combined total at $176,100 would be wrong in both directions. No rounding here - the products round at lines 2, 4 and 6.

Fact.Name: This employee's contribution to Schedule H line 3
Fact.Description:
The employee's whole cash wages when they reach lines 1, 3 and 5, with NO cap: "Enter the total cash wages (see Cash wages, earlier) paid in 2025 to each employee who meets the $2,800 test, explained earlier. There is no limit on wages subject to Medicare tax" (https://www.irs.gov/pub/irs-pdf/i1040sh.pdf, page 5).
THIS IS WHY LINE 3 IS NEVER LESS THAN LINE 1, a relation the retired attestations could not hold: same employee set, same wage figure, one capped and one not.

Fact.Name: This employee's contribution to Schedule H line 5
Fact.Description:
The EXCESS over the Additional Medicare Tax withholding threshold, not the whole wage: "Enter the total cash wages (see Cash wages, earlier) paid to each employee in 2025 that exceeded $200,000" (https://www.irs.gov/pub/irs-pdf/i1040sh.pdf, page 5).
EXCEEDED, SO THE BOUNDARY EMPLOYEE AT EXACTLY $200,000.00 CONTRIBUTES NOTHING; the one at $200,000.01 contributes a cent. The floor at zero is what "that exceeded" means for every employee below the threshold.

Fact.Name: This employee's contribution to Schedule H lines 15 and 20
Fact.Description:
The employee's cash wages capped at the FUTA base: "If you paid any household employee more than $7,000 in 2025, include on line 15 only the first $7,000 of that employee's cash wages" (https://www.irs.gov/pub/irs-pdf/i1040sh.pdf, page 6).
A DIFFERENT WAGE BASE FROM LINES 1 AND 3 IN THREE WAYS, all printed: no $2,800 floor ("including employees paid less than $1,000", lines 364-366), a SHORTER exclusion list (../isExcludedFromFutaWages), and a $7,000 rather than $176,100 cap.

Fact.Name: This employee was employed by the primary filer
Fact.Description: The primary half of the employer attribution, built to the shape formW2s:/formW2s/*/belongsToPrimaryFiler uses. AN UNANSWERED ../writableEmployerFiler counts as the primary filer, which is exact for the single-employer return: with one employer there is one schedule and the attribution question is never asked.

Fact.Name: This employee was employed by the secondary filer
Fact.Description: The secondary half of the employer attribution. It requires an ANSWERED ../writableEmployerFiler, the mirror of ../belongsToPrimaryFiler's default, so that every row belongs to exactly one filer.

Fact.Name: This employee row is missing an answer the graph cannot safely default
Fact.Description:
The per-row completeness guard, built to the shape /scheduleHFutaStateContributions/*/rowIsIncomplete uses and refusing the SAME direction: every clause here is an omission whose default would UNDER-state the tax.
(1) NO CASH WAGES. ../cashWages defaults to zero, which shrinks all four lines.
(2) A PARENT ROW WITH EITHER EXCEPTION CONDITION UNANSWERED. The default excludes the parent from lines 1, 3 and 5 ("Exception for parents", https://www.irs.gov/pub/irs-pdf/i1040sh.pdf, page 4), so an unanswered condition buys the filer an exclusion they may not have.
(3) AN UNDER-18 ROW WHOSE EXCEPTION IS UNRESOLVED. Answered under-18 excludes by default, and the printed exception can put the employee back (lines 265-268). The student answer is required of every under-18 row; the principal-occupation answer only of a NON-student, because a student is excluded whatever their occupation.
(4) TRANSPORTATION REIMBURSEMENTS LARGER THAN THE CASH WAGES. The reimbursements are part of the cash wages paid (lines 296-311), so an excludable amount above the wage figure contradicts it; flooring the employee at zero would drop wages the filer may have mis-entered.
WHAT IS DELIBERATELY NOT HERE: an unanswered RELATIONSHIP. It resolves as `other`, which INCLUDES the employee everywhere and over-states the tax - the direction this module does not refuse (/knockoutScheduleHRequiredButIncomplete). Adding it would be new policy, not a bug fix.

Fact.Name: Line 1 total across the household employees
Fact.Description:
The sum of every row's ../line1Wages - the number the retired /writableScheduleHLine1CashWagesSubjectToSocialSecurityTax used to attest. An EMPTY collection sums to a Complete zero, which is what makes every Schedule H line complete-safe; the guard that stops a zero from becoming a silent filing is /scheduleHPartIAnswersAreComplete, not this fact.
AN UNANSWERED COLLECTION IS NOT AN EMPTY ONE, and this fact carries an explicit zero arm for the difference. A CollectionSum over an ANSWERED empty /householdEmployees is a Complete zero; over a collection that was never answered at all it is Incomplete, and that Incompleteness propagated straight through the gated line into /knockoutScheduleHRequiredButIncomplete, which stopped resolving - a refusal silently DISARMED rather than a visible failure.

Fact.Description:

AN UNANSWERED COLLECTION IS NOT AN EMPTY ONE, and this fact carries an explicit zero arm for the difference. Fact.Name: Lines 15 and 20 total across the household employees
Fact.Description:
The sum of every row's ../line15Wages. ONE TOTAL FOR TWO PRINTED BOXES, exactly as one writable served both before this landing: line 15 is asked of the Section A filer and line 20 of the Section B filer, on mutually exclusive routes, and line 20's own printed text is "Total cash wages subject to FUTA tax (see the line 15 instructions)" (https://www.irs.gov/pub/irs-pdf/f1040sh.pdf, page 2).
AN UNANSWERED COLLECTION IS NOT AN EMPTY ONE, and this fact carries an explicit zero arm for the difference. A CollectionSum over an ANSWERED empty /householdEmployees is a Complete zero; over a collection that was never answered at all it is Incomplete, and that Incompleteness propagated straight through the gated line into /knockoutScheduleHRequiredButIncomplete, which stopped resolving - a refusal silently DISARMED rather than a visible failure. EXPORTED RATHER THAN CONSUMED, and that is a consequence of the per-filer routing split rather than a design intent. Its two consumers were the return-level lines 15 and 20, and both are now rollups over /filers/* whose per-filer arms read the NAMED primary/secondary employee collections directly - the engine cannot Filter a collection by the current outer item, so a per-filer step cannot go through a return-level total. It is kept because it is a Complete row on all 939 committed cases (retiring it would REMOVE 939 rows, a changed store rather than an additive one) and because it remains the true combined figure the application surface shows above two printed schedules: every employee lands on exactly one route, so /scheduleHLine15 plus /scheduleHLine20 equals this total on any return.

Fact.Name: At least one household employee row is unfinished
Fact.Description:
Whether /scheduleHHouseholdEmployeesIncompleteRows is non-empty. Read by both completeness predicates, so an unfinished row refuses the return on either Part's route.
AN UNANSWERED COLLECTION IS NOT AN EMPTY ONE, and this fact carries an explicit FALSE arm for the difference (see /scheduleHHouseholdEmployeesLine1Total for the measurement). FALSE is the REFUSING arm here, which is the same answer the answered-but-empty collection gives, so the guard never buys a filer a filing they could not otherwise have.

Fact.Name: Household employees whose wages reach lines 1, 3 and 5
Fact.Description: The subset of /householdEmployees whose ../countsForSocialSecurityAndMedicare is true - the employees line A is asking about.

Fact.Name: The employee list contains someone line A's Yes could be about
Fact.Description:
Whether at least one listed employee is both ON line A's list and at or above $2,800. THIS IS LINE A's OWN QUESTION, asked of the collection instead of the filer: "Did you pay any one household employee cash wages of $2,800 or more in 2025?" (https://www.irs.gov/pub/irs-pdf/f1040sh.pdf, page 1), and its instruction applies the same exclusion list ("To figure the total cash wages you paid in 2025 to each household employee, don't include amounts paid to any of the following individuals", https://www.irs.gov/pub/irs-pdf/i1040sh.pdf, page 4). So a Yes on line A is true exactly when this fact is.
WHAT IT COSTS, STATED PLAINLY. /scheduleHPartIAnswersAreComplete reads it, so a filer who checks Yes on line A and then lists no qualifying employee is REFUSED rather than filed with $0 of social security tax. That population could file before this landing (they answered the four attestations with zeros); the refusal is new, it is narrow, and it runs in the module's established direction - a Yes on line A with nothing behind it is an UNDER-statement with no other guard reaching it, because lines 1 through 6 would all be complete-safe zeros. It stays a completeness guard, not a scope refusal: the return is unfinished, not unmodelled.
AN UNANSWERED COLLECTION IS NOT AN EMPTY ONE, and this fact carries an explicit FALSE arm for the difference (see /scheduleHHouseholdEmployeesLine1Total for the measurement). FALSE is the REFUSING arm here, which is the same answer the answered-but-empty collection gives, so the guard never buys a filer a filing they could not otherwise have.

Fact.Name: The filer has listed at least one household employee
Fact.Description:
Whether /householdEmployees is non-empty. THE PART II COUNTERPART OF /scheduleHHouseholdEmployeesSupportLineA, and deliberately weaker than it: Part II is entered on the $1,000-quarter test ("if you paid total cash wages of $1,000 or more in any calendar quarter of 2024 or 2025 to household employees", https://www.irs.gov/pub/irs-pdf/i1040sh.pdf, page 6), which asserts that employees exist but sets no per-employee floor, and line 15's own instruction expressly counts "employees paid less than $1,000" (lines 364-366). So the Part II guard asks only that the employees be LISTED, never that any of them clear a threshold.
WHY A GUARD IS OWED AT ALL: lines 15 and 20 are now CollectionSums, and a sum over an empty collection is a Complete zero. Without this test a Part II filer with no employee rows would file 0.6% of zero (Section A) or a zero line 24 (Section B) with nothing refusing them - the exact hole /knockoutScheduleHRequiredButIncomplete arm 2 is widened to close, re-expressed against the collection that replaced the attestation.
AN UNANSWERED COLLECTION IS NOT AN EMPTY ONE, and this fact carries an explicit FALSE arm for the difference (see /scheduleHHouseholdEmployeesLine1Total for the measurement). FALSE is the REFUSING arm here, which is the same answer the answered-but-empty collection gives, so the guard never buys a filer a filing they could not otherwise have.

Fact.Name: This employee's wages belong on a Schedule H this return carries
Fact.Description:
True on a joint return, where both spouses' schedules are attached to this Form 1040. On a return that is not filing jointly there is ONE taxpayer and therefore one Schedule H, so an employee attributed to the secondary filer belongs on a schedule this return does not carry.
THE SECONDARY TEST RATHER THAN ../belongsToPrimaryFiler, and the two are not interchangeable here: ../belongsToPrimaryFiler reads filers:/primaryFiler, which is a Find and is unresolvable while the primary/secondary designation is unanswered. An unattributed row is the primary filer's by the module's own default and stays on the return.
This paragraph used to end "../belongsToSecondaryFiler requires an ANSWERED ../writableEmployerFiler, so its negation is the complete-safe side". That is FALSE as written, and the sentence was the prose form of the defect finding B1 measured. ../belongsToSecondaryFiler is All(IsComplete(../writableEmployerFiler), Equal(../writableEmployerFiler, filers:/secondaryFiler)), so it is complete-safe only when the attribution is UNANSWERED — the All then has a false operand to short-circuit on. When the attribution IS answered and filers:/secondaryFiler does not resolve, the Equal never resolves, the All has no false operand, and the read is unresolvable. Records state what IS.
TWO ARMS ARE GUARDED, NOT ONE, and each guard is a measured defect rather than decoration. (1) AN UNANSWERED FILING STATUS TAKES THE INCLUDING ARM: a bare Any(MFJ, Not(../belongsToSecondaryFiler)) is INCOMPLETE for exactly the row this fact exists to judge — an employee attributed to the secondary filer on a return whose /filingStatus has not been answered — because the Any has no true operand to short-circuit on. (2) AN UNRESOLVABLE ATTRIBUTION TAKES IT TOO: with /filingStatus answered non-MFJ, an ANSWERED ../writableEmployerFiler on a return where filers:/secondaryFiler does not resolve made this Switch Placeholder. That is a REACHABLE mid-interview state — nothing in this dictionary sequences ../writableEmployerFiler after the primary/secondary designation, and there is no flowShouldAsk gate on it at all. Either Incompleteness reaches ../countsForSocialSecurityAndMedicare, and from there lines 1, 3 and 5, /scheduleHHouseholdEmployeesSupportLineA, /scheduleHPartIAnswersAreComplete and /knockoutScheduleHRequiredButIncomplete — i.e. it silently DISARMS the module's completeness refusal AND stops Part I's money resolving, rather than failing visibly. All 46 committed scheduleH fixtures carry two /filers entries with isPrimaryFiler answered on both, so no fixture would have caught either. TRUE IS THE RIGHT ARM FOR BOTH, and the direction is the argument: including everyone is the historical behaviour, so an unknown can only leave the return where it already was — never silently delete a schedule's wages.
Sign: this fact only ever REMOVES wages from the return's lines, never adds any.

Fact.Name: Household employees whose wages belong on a Schedule H this return carries
Fact.Description: The subset of /householdEmployees whose ../belongsOnThisReturn is true. A filter rather than a count, for the same reason /scheduleHHouseholdEmployeesIncompleteRows is one: the application surface renders the schedules and needs the identities.

Fact.Name: Household employees are attributed to both filers
Fact.Description:
THE SIGNAL THIS GRAPH DID NOT HOLD BEFORE THIS LANDING, and its absence was the stated reason module header scope item (4) carried a declared residual rather than a refusal: "the graph holds no signal that a return has two household employers ... Form 2441 column (d) identifies care providers, not which spouse employs them". The employee collection with its ../writableEmployerFiler attribution is that signal, so the claim is retired here and in the header.
WHAT IT CLAIMS IS EXACTLY WHAT IT COMPUTES, and the distinction matters enough to spell out: employees are attributed to BOTH filers. It does NOT claim that two Schedules H are owed, because it does NOT test the filing status. "Only two Schedules H can be attached to Form 1040, 1040-SR, and 1040-SS, one Schedule H for each of the primary taxpayer and the secondary taxpayer" (https://www.irs.gov/pub/irs-pdf/i1040sh.pdf, page 4) presupposes a joint return; a SINGLE return with a stray secondary attribution has one schedule and a mis-attributed employee, which is the /dividendReports/secondaryFilerUsedWithoutMFJ class rather than this one. No dollar moves on it today - all four totals sum across every employee whatever their attribution - so the guard is owed by whatever change first makes the attribution move money, and the successor contract's obligation (a) names it. The FORM SPLIT is a rendering concern the application surface owns (invariant #7), which is why this fact is exported rather than consumed here.
WHAT IT LED TO. This paragraph used to end "WHAT IT DOES NOT DO YET: split the computation", and that successor landed the same day: Section B's line 23 now caps the state unemployment credit once per SCHEDULE (/filers/*/scheduleHLine23, rolled up here), which closes the under-statement this fact's existence made buildable. What remains: Section A's line 16 still rounds once per return, and the Part II routing is still return-level.
IT IS NOT A FILING-STATUS TEST, and the distinction it draws above is exactly why: this fact says employees are attributed to both filers, not that the return is joint. What a secondary attribution means on a NON-joint return is answered by /householdEmployees/*/belongsOnThisReturn and /filers/*/scheduleHBelongsOnThisReturn, which keep those records off the one schedule such a return carries; the refusal that stood there from the per-filer fill until then is retired.

Fact.Name: Schedule H line 1, derived from the household employee collection
Fact.Description:
Line 1, gated on line A and complete-safe to zero. Lines 1 through 6 are reached only through line A's "Yes. Skip lines B and C and go to line 1" (https://www.irs.gov/pub/irs-pdf/f1040sh.pdf, page 1): a filer who answered No to A and Yes to B goes to line 7 directly, and a filer routed through line C skips lines 1 through 9 altogether. So social security wages are entered only on the line-A path, and this Switch is that routing, not a safety wrapper bolted on afterwards.
DERIVED, NOT ATTESTED. The value arm was /writableScheduleHLine1CashWagesSubjectToSocialSecurityTax, a return-level total the graph could not test against either of the line's two printed per-employee rules. It is now /scheduleHHouseholdEmployeesLine1Total, the sum over /householdEmployees of each employee's wages capped at the $176,100 social security base, counting only employees who are on line A's list and meet the $2,800 test. The attestation is retired; see git history at this file.
THE ZERO ARM IS BOTH: it is the printed routing AND the unanswered-safe default, because a return that never saw line A resolves /scheduleHLineA false. It no longer needs an IsComplete leg, because a CollectionSum over an empty collection is a Complete zero - which is why /scheduleHPartIAnswersAreComplete had to grow a collection-side test in the same landing.

Fact.Name: Social security tax (Schedule H line 2)
Fact.Description:
Schedule H line 2: "Social security tax. Multiply line 1 by 12.4% (0.124)" (https://www.irs.gov/pub/irs-pdf/f1040sh.pdf, page 1), restated in the instruction as "Multiply the amount on line 1 by 12.4% (0.124). Enter the result on line 2" (https://www.irs.gov/pub/irs-pdf/i1040sh.pdf, page 5).
WHY 12.4% AND NOT 6.2%. The household employer owes BOTH shares. "For 2025, the rate of social security tax on taxable wages is 6.2% each for the employee and employer" (https://www.irs.gov/pub/irs-pdf/i1040sh.pdf, page 5), and "If you didn't deduct the employee's share from the employee's wages, you must pay the employee's share of tax and your share of tax, a total of 12.4% for social security tax and 2.9% for Medicare tax" (lines 339-342). The printed line takes the combined rate unconditionally, so this fact does too - whether the employer actually withheld the employee's half changes the Form W-2 boxes, never this line.
ROUNDED PER SCHEDULE, HALF-UP to whole dollars: each printed schedule rounds its own line 2 (/filers/*/scheduleHLine2), and this return-level line adds them. When some employee on the return is not on either filer's schedule (an unreadable filer role), it falls back to one Round over /scheduleHLine1. Sign: NON-NEGATIVE.

Fact.Description:

LINE 3 IS NOW STRUCTURALLY AT LEAST LINE 1, which the two retired attestations could not guarantee and which no Limit could have expressed between them.

Multiply line 3 by 2.9% (0.029)" (https://www.irs.gov/pub/irs-pdf/f1040sh.pdf, page 1). 2.9% is again the COMBINED rate - "The Medicare tax rate is 1.45% each for the employee and employer, unchanged from 2024. There is no wage base limit for Medicare tax" (https://www.irs.gov/pub/irs-pdf/i1040sh.pdf, page 5) - for the same reason line 2 takes 12.4%.
ROUNDED PER SCHEDULE, HALF-UP, and added here, with the fallback /scheduleHLine2 describes. Sign: NON-NEGATIVE.

Fact.Name: Additional Medicare Tax withholding (Schedule H line 6)

The household employer owes it because they were required to withhold it - "you must withhold a 0.9% Additional Medicare Tax from wages you pay to an employee in excess of $200,000 in a calendar year" (https://www.irs.gov/pub/irs-pdf/i1040sh.pdf, page 5).

Fact.Name: Federal income tax withheld, if any (this filer's Schedule H line 7)
Fact.Description:
Schedule H line 7 on THIS filer's own schedule: "Federal income tax withheld, if any" (https://www.irs.gov/pub/irs-pdf/f1040sh.pdf, page 1). "Enter any federal income tax you withheld from the wages you paid to your household employees in 2025" (https://www.irs.gov/pub/irs-pdf/i1040sh.pdf, page 5).
A TAX ON THIS SCHEDULE, NOT A PAYMENT ON THE RETURN. Line 7 is the income tax the EMPLOYER withheld from the EMPLOYEE and now owes over to the Treasury; it flows into line 8 and thence into Schedule 2 line 9 as a tax. It is not the filer's own withholding and must never reach Form 1040 line 25 - the employee claims it on their own return, from their own Form W-2.
Income tax withheld from an employee whose taxes are reported on a business Form 941, 943 or 944 or by a section 3504 agent is reported there and is left out of this line.
PUERTO RICO: skipped ("Household employers located in Puerto Rico, skip line 7", https://www.irs.gov/pub/irs-pdf/i1040sh.pdf, page 5). Leaving this unanswered is exactly what skipping it means, so no separate handling is owed (module header scope item 5).
ONE ANSWER PER SCHEDULE. "Only two Schedules H can be attached to Form 1040, 1040-SR, and 1040-SS, one Schedule H for each of the primary taxpayer and the secondary taxpayer" (https://www.irs.gov/pub/irs-pdf/i1040sh.pdf, page 4), and each spouse's line 7 is the income tax THAT spouse withheld from the employees THAT spouse employed. The return-level /scheduleHLine7 adds the answers of the filers whose schedules the return carries, so a single-employer return answers it once, on the employer's filer. Sign: NON-NEGATIVE.

Fact.Name: Schedule H line 7 on this filer's own schedule
Fact.Description: Line 7 as THIS filer's schedule prints it: ../writableScheduleHLine7FederalIncomeTaxWithheld when the printed routing reaches line 7 and the schedule is one this return carries, else zero. Line A's Yes routes into Part I as a whole ("Yes. Skip lines B and C and go to line 1"), which reaches line 7 in sequence; line B's Yes routes to it directly ("Yes. Skip line C and go to line 7"). Source: https://www.irs.gov/pub/irs-pdf/f1040sh.pdf, page 1. A line-C filer never reaches line 7 - "Yes. Skip lines 1-9 and go to line 10" (line 33). THE ROUTE IS READ AT THE RETURN, as /scheduleHLine1 through /filers/*/scheduleHLine6 read it: Part I is entered when the return answered line A or line B Yes, and each filer's schedule then carries that filer's own entries. Complete-safe to zero.
