Fact.Name: Schedule H line 7 is answered on a schedule this return carries
Fact.Description: True when at least one filer whose schedule this return carries answered line 7. It is the test /scheduleHPartIAnswersAreComplete applies to line 7, which stays an attestation because the income tax an employer withheld is not derivable from wages. ONE answer on the return satisfies it, which is the test the return-level line 7 answer met before line 7 moved under /filers/*: on a joint return with two household employers each spouse's own line 7 is asked, and an unanswered one reads zero. Complete-safe false on an unanswered /filers.

Fact.Name: Schedule H line 7 as entered
Fact.Description: Line 7 for the return: the line 7 of every schedule this return carries, added (/filers/*/scheduleHLine7, each already zero off the Part I route, for a filer whose schedule the return does not carry, and when unanswered). On a single-employer return that is the employer's one line 7. Reached by EITHER printed path, line A's Yes or line B's Yes (https://www.irs.gov/pub/irs-pdf/f1040sh.pdf, page 1); a line-C filer never reaches it ("Yes. Skip lines 1-9 and go to line 10", line 33). Complete-safe to zero, including on a return whose /filers is unanswered.

Fact.Name: Social security and Medicare taxes withheld by a state disability plan (this filer's schedule)
Fact.Description:
The line 8 adjustment the printed form does not carry but the instructions require. "Certain state disability plan payments to household employees are treated as wages subject to social security and Medicare taxes. If your employee received payments from a plan that withheld the employee's share of social security and Medicare taxes, include the payments on lines 1, 3, and, if applicable, 5 of Schedule H and complete the rest of Part I through line 7. Add lines 2, 4, 6, and 7. ... From that total, subtract the amount of these taxes withheld by the state. Enter the result on line 8. Also, enter 'disability' and the amount subtracted on the dotted line next to line 8" (https://www.irs.gov/pub/irs-pdf/i1040sh.pdf, page 10).
MODELLED RATHER THAN OMITTED, and the direction is why. Omitting it would leave line 8 at the printed sum for a population whose line 8 is smaller than that sum, i.e. an OVER-stated tax. Carrying it as a zero-defaulting intake is identical to the printed sum on every return that does not answer it, and correct on the ones that do. No intake asks it today (SERVICE-owned, invariant #7). ONE ANSWER PER SCHEDULE: the subtraction belongs on the line 8 of the schedule that lists the employee the state plan paid, so it is asked of the filer who employed that employee; /scheduleHStateDisabilityPlanTaxesWithheld adds the answers of the schedules the return carries. Sign: NON-NEGATIVE (an amount withheld).

Fact.Name: State disability plan withholding on this filer's schedule, complete-safe
Fact.Description: This filer's line 8 disability subtraction (../writableScheduleHStateDisabilityPlanTaxesWithheld) with unanswered read as zero, and zero for a filer whose schedule this return does not carry.

Fact.Name: State disability plan withholding, complete-safe
Fact.Description: The line 8 disability subtraction for the return: each carried schedule's own subtraction (/filers/*/scheduleHStateDisabilityPlanTaxesWithheld) added, zero when none is answered and on a return whose /filers is unanswered.

Fact.Name: Total social security, Medicare, and federal income taxes (Schedule H line 8)
Fact.Description:
Schedule H line 8: "Total social security, Medicare, and federal income taxes. Add lines 2, 4, 6, and 7" (https://www.irs.gov/pub/irs-pdf/f1040sh.pdf, page 1), less the state disability plan withholding the instruction subtracts here (/scheduleHStateDisabilityPlanTaxesWithheld, zero on every return that does not answer it).
FLOORED AT ZERO, and this is a reading rather than a printed rule. The instruction's subtraction carries no "if zero or less, enter -0-" and cannot go negative in practice: the amount a state plan withholds is at most the employee's share, i.e. at most half of lines 2 and 4 combined. The floor exists so that a mis-entered subtraction cannot produce a NEGATIVE household employment tax, which would reduce Form 1040 line 23 below the other taxes actually owed - an outcome no reading of Schedule H supports. interpretation:provisional.
ROUNDED HERE. The four addends are each already whole-dollar printed entries, so the Round is a no-op on the standard path; it binds only when the disability subtraction carries cents.

Fact.Name: Every Part I line the routing requires has been answered
Fact.Description:
Whether the filer who reached Part I actually supplied its entries. On the line-A path the employee list must carry someone line A's Yes could be about and must be finished, and line 7 must be answered; on the line-B-only path just line 7 is required, since lines 1 through 6 are skipped. A filer who reached neither path owes nothing and is trivially complete.
REWRITTEN FOR LINES 1, 3 AND 5 NO LONGER BEING ATTESTATIONS. The three IsComplete legs that used to stand here tested the four retired writables; ported naively they would have become VACUOUS, because lines 1, 3 and 5 are now CollectionSums and a sum over an empty collection is a Complete zero. A line-A Yes with no employees listed would then have filed $0 of social security tax with nothing refusing it - the precise under-statement this predicate exists to prevent. The collection-side tests (/scheduleHHouseholdEmployeesSupportLineA for "somebody is behind that Yes", /scheduleHHouseholdEmployeesHaveIncompleteRow for "and their rows are finished") are what carry that protection now.
LINE 7 KEEPS ITS OWN IsComplete because it is still an attestation: the income tax the employer withheld is not derivable from wages.
THIS IS THE PREDICATE /knockoutScheduleHRequiredButIncomplete NEGATES.

Fact.Name: Part II (FUTA) is entered
Fact.Description: Part II is entered exactly when the $1,000-quarter test is met: "You need to pay federal unemployment tax under the FUTA, if you paid total cash wages of $1,000 or more in any calendar quarter of 2024 or 2025 to household employees" (https://www.irs.gov/pub/irs-pdf/i1040sh.pdf, page 6). Both printed routes agree - line C's "Yes. Skip lines 1-9 and go to line 10" and line 9's "Yes. Go to line 10" - which is why one writable serves both boxes.

Fact.Name: Did this filer pay unemployment contributions to only one state?
Fact.Description:
Schedule H line 10 on THIS filer's own schedule: "Did you pay unemployment contributions to only one state? If you paid contributions to a credit reduction state, see instructions and check 'No'" (https://www.irs.gov/pub/irs-pdf/f1040sh.pdf, page 2).
THE SECOND SENTENCE IS LOAD-BEARING. It routes every credit-reduction-state filer into Section B, where the reduction is applied rather than avoided. For 2025 the affected jurisdictions are California (reduction rate 0.012) and the U.S. Virgin Islands (0.045); every other jurisdiction's rate is 0.000 (https://www.irs.gov/pub/irs-pdf/i1040sh.pdf, page 9), and those rates are read off the printed table at /scheduleHFutaStateContributions/*/creditReduction.
PER FILER; the retired return-level twin is recorded above. The question is asked once per SCHEDULE, so on an MFJ return with two household employers each spouse answers their own and one spouse's No no longer drags the other into Section B.
UNANSWERED READS AS "not established", which reaches neither section: see ../scheduleHFutaSectionBApplies, which requires all three of lines 10-12 to be ANSWERED, and /scheduleHPartIIAnswersAreComplete, which refuses the filer whose own schedule reaches Part II with their own three unanswered.

Fact.Name: Did this filer pay all state unemployment contributions for 2025 by April 15, 2026?
Fact.Description:
Schedule H line 11 on THIS filer's own schedule: "Did you pay all state unemployment contributions for 2025 by April 15, 2026? Fiscal year filers, see instructions" (https://www.irs.gov/pub/irs-pdf/f1040sh.pdf, page 2). A No routes this filer to Section B and to their own Worksheet 1, because a late payment cuts the credit to 90% of what it would have been (https://www.irs.gov/pub/irs-pdf/i1040sh.pdf, page 6).
PER FILER. One spouse paying late says nothing about the other's schedule, and the Worksheet 1 chain this answer drives is already per filer (/filers/*/scheduleHFutaWorksheet1Line1 through .../Line8). Unanswered reads as "not established", which routes to the same refusal.

Fact.Name: Were all of this filer's FUTA-taxable wages also taxable for their state's unemployment tax?
Fact.Description:
Schedule H line 12 on THIS filer's own schedule: "Were all wages that are taxable for FUTA tax also taxable for your state's unemployment tax?" (https://www.irs.gov/pub/irs-pdf/f1040sh.pdf, page 2). A No means part of THIS filer's FUTA base carried no state contribution, so the flat 5.4% credit Section A assumes does not hold for their schedule and Section B's column-by-column computation is required of it.
PER FILER, for the same reason as its two siblings: the wage base the question is about is this filer's own line 20, which the sibling landing already made per filer. Unanswered reads as "not established", which routes to the same refusal.

Fact.Name: This filer's Schedule H is one of the schedules this return carries
Fact.Description:
"Only two Schedules H can be attached to Form 1040, 1040-SR, and 1040-SS, one Schedule H for each of the primary taxpayer and the secondary taxpayer" (https://www.irs.gov/pub/irs-pdf/i1040sh.pdf, page 4) PRESUPPOSES a joint return: a return that is not filing jointly has one taxpayer, so it carries the primary filer's schedule and no other.
THE MFJ ARM COMES FIRST AND SHORT-CIRCUITS, which is what makes this fact safe to read from the per-filer chain. ../isPrimaryFiler is a Writable and ../isSecondaryFiler is Derived through a Find, so a filer missing either would take a bare two-arm Switch Incomplete - and /scheduleHTotalHouseholdEmploymentTaxes is exported into taxCalculations, where an Incompleteness would move Schedule 2 on every return in the corpus. That is the lesson the per-filer routing recorded, and this Switch obeys it: every arm is guarded by its own IsComplete and the Switch ends in a True arm.
THE TRUE TAIL IS THE INCLUDING ONE, deliberately. A filer whose primary/secondary role cannot be read is kept ON the return, so an unreadable role can never silently delete a schedule's wages; it can only leave the pre-existing behaviour in place.
AN UNANSWERED FILING STATUS GETS ITS OWN FIRST ARM, for the same reason and against the same failure. A Switch whose first When read filingStatus:/isFilingStatusMFJ bare would be INCOMPLETE on a return that has not answered filing status, and that Incompleteness would reach ../scheduleHFutaSectionAApplies, ../scheduleHFutaSectionBApplies and ../scheduleHPartIIAnswersAreIncomplete, whose own first case negates this fact — i.e. it would silently DISARM /knockoutScheduleHRequiredButIncomplete mid-interview rather than fail visibly, which is the shape /scheduleHHouseholdEmployeesLine1Total's own Description records as the module's most expensive prior bug. Every committed case answers filing status, so no fixture would have caught it. TRUE is the right unknown-status arm: it keeps every filer on the return, which is exactly the historical behaviour.

Fact.Name: FUTA Section A applies on this filer's own schedule (their lines 10, 11 and 12 all answered Yes)
Fact.Description:
"Next: If you checked the 'Yes' box on all the lines above, complete Section A. If you checked the 'No' box on any of the lines above, skip Section A and complete Section B" (https://www.irs.gov/pub/irs-pdf/f1040sh.pdf, page 2), read off THIS filer's own three answers.
THE PART II GATE STAYS RETURN-LEVEL and that is the printed reading, not a shortcut. /scheduleHFutaApplies is the $1,000-quarter test, which lines C and 9 ask about "total cash wages ... to household employees" - all of them, on the one Form 1040 - rather than per schedule. A filer who reaches Part II but employs nobody has a line 15 of zero by their own gating, so nothing rides on the difference.
UNANSWERED IS NOT YES. Each of the three arms is the complete-safe reading of its writable, so a filer who has answered none of their own lines 10-12 fails this predicate. They are not routed into Section A's flat 0.6%, and they do not reach Section B either (../scheduleHFutaSectionBApplies requires all three ANSWERED); they are refused by arm 2 of /knockoutScheduleHRequiredButIncomplete, through ../scheduleHPartIIAnswersAreIncomplete. That is the world-1 direction: Section A's rate is the LOWEST the schedule can produce, so defaulting into it would under-state FUTA by up to 5.4% of the FUTA wage base.

Fact.Name: FUTA Section B applies on this filer's own schedule (a No on their line 10, 11 or 12, all three answered)
Fact.Description:
"Complete lines 17 through 24 only if you checked a 'No' box on line 10, 11, or 12" (https://www.irs.gov/pub/irs-pdf/i1040sh.pdf, page 6), the caution that mirrors the form's own "If you checked the 'No' box on any of the lines above, skip Section A and complete Section B" (https://www.irs.gov/pub/irs-pdf/f1040sh.pdf, page 2) - read off THIS filer's own three answers.
THIS IS THE FACT THE PER-FILER SECTION B CHAIN GATES ON. Every step of that chain used to read the RETURN-LEVEL predicate, which is what made one spouse's No reroute the other's schedule. The four collection-reaching steps and the sixteen arithmetic ones below now read ../ instead.
ALL THREE MUST BE ANSWERED, and that requirement is the structural home of the direction argument the retired /knockoutScheduleHFutaSectionB used to carry in prose. A filer who has answered NONE of their own lines 10-12 satisfies neither ../scheduleHFutaSectionAApplies (which needs three answered Yeses) nor this predicate, so their schedule computes nothing and the return is refused by /knockoutScheduleHRequiredButIncomplete instead. That is the safe direction: Section A produces the LOWEST FUTA figure the schedule can (0.6% against a 6.0% gross rate), so defaulting an unanswered question into it would systematically under-state.
IT ALSO MATTERS THAT LINE 11 IS ANSWERED SPECIFICALLY. Line 11 is the printed late-payment question, and this filer's Worksheet 1 runs only on a No. An unanswered line 11 would leave "were you late?" unknown while the arithmetic proceeded as though the answer were Yes.

Fact.Name: Filers whose own Schedule H completes Section A
Fact.Description: The subset of /filers whose ../scheduleHFutaSectionAApplies is true. A filter rather than a count, for the same reason /scheduleHFutaIncompleteRows is one: the application surface renders one schedule per member and needs their identities, not a tally. The engine has no boolean any-over-collection operator, so this pair (filter, then size test) is how the return-level predicate below is expressed at all.

Fact.Name: At least one filer's Schedule H completes Section A
Fact.Description:
This fact is a rollup, and its MEANING CHANGED with it - the one thing about this landing a reader must not misread. This fact used to BE the Section A routing, computed once for the whole return from three return-level writables. It is now "at least one filer's schedule reaches Section A", over /filersReachingScheduleHFutaSectionA. On a return whose two spouses route differently this AND /scheduleHFutaSectionBApplies are both true at once, which is exactly the population the split exists for and would have been a contradiction before it.
NOTHING IN THIS GRAPH READS IT ANY MORE, and it is EXPORTED rather than consumed for exactly the reason /scheduleHReturnHasTwoHouseholdEmployers is: which sections a return's schedules print is a rendering question the application surface owns (invariant #7). Section A's arithmetic gates on /filers/*/scheduleHFutaSectionAApplies (see /filers/*/scheduleHLine15) and Section B's on the per-filer twin, and the completeness guard needs only the Section B side (to decide whether the line 17 rows must be finished), so the rebody took this fact's last in-graph consumer with it. It is kept rather than retired because it is a Complete row on all 939 committed cases and retiring it would REMOVE 939 rows - a changed store, not an additive one. THE IsComplete(/filers) GUARD WITH AN EXPLICIT FALSE ARM is what keeps this a COMPLETE false rather than a Placeholder one on a return that answers nothing at all - a Filter over an unanswered collection resolves Placeholder, and this fact was a Complete false on every committed case before the rebody.

Fact.Name: Filers whose own Schedule H completes Section B
Fact.Description: The subset of /filers whose ../scheduleHFutaSectionBApplies is true. See /filersReachingScheduleHFutaSectionA for why the pair exists.

Fact.Name: At least one filer's Schedule H completes Section B
Fact.Description:
This fact is a rollup over /filersReachingScheduleHFutaSectionB, exactly as /scheduleHFutaSectionAApplies was, and with the same change of meaning: "at least one filer's schedule reaches Section B" rather than "the return is a Section B return". The two can now be true together.
ITS ONE REMAINING CONSUMER IS THE COMPLETENESS GUARD. /scheduleHPartIIAnswersAreComplete requires every line 17 row to be finished only when some schedule on the return actually reaches Section B, which is what this fact answers. Every dollar that used to read it now reads /filers/*/scheduleHFutaSectionBApplies: the two line 18 totals, line 20 and Worksheet 2 line 4 were repointed in the same landing.
THE IsComplete(/filers) GUARD WITH AN EXPLICIT FALSE ARM keeps it a COMPLETE false on a return that answers nothing (see the sibling above).

Fact.Name: Name of the state where you paid unemployment contributions (this filer's Schedule H line 13)
Fact.Description:
Schedule H Section A line 13: "Name of the state where you paid unemployment contributions" (https://www.irs.gov/pub/irs-pdf/f1040sh.pdf, page 2). "Enter the two-letter abbreviation of the name of the state (or the District of Columbia, Puerto Rico, or the U.S. Virgin Islands) to which you paid unemployment contributions" (https://www.irs.gov/pub/irs-pdf/i1040sh.pdf, page 6).
A DISCLOSURE FIELD - no dollar on this schedule reads it. Line 16 is a flat 0.6% of line 15 regardless of which state the contributions went to; the state identity matters only inside Section B's Worksheet 2, which this module refuses. It is carried here so the printed schedule can be filled and exported rather than silently left blank, and its presence must not be read as state-tax scope (invariant #7): this is a federal FUTA disclosure of a state name, not any state computation. ONE ANSWER PER SCHEDULE: Section A is reached on a filer's own schedule by that filer's own lines 10-12 (/filers/*/scheduleHFutaSectionAApplies), and on a joint return with two household employers each spouse names the state that spouse paid.

Fact.Name: Contributions paid to your state unemployment fund (this filer's Schedule H line 14)
Fact.Description:
Schedule H Section A line 14: "Contributions paid to your state unemployment fund" (https://www.irs.gov/pub/irs-pdf/f1040sh.pdf, page 2). "Enter the total of contributions (defined earlier) you paid to your state unemployment fund for 2025. If you didn't have to make contributions because your state gave you a 0% experience rate, enter '0% rate' on line 14" (https://www.irs.gov/pub/irs-pdf/i1040sh.pdf, page 6).
A DISCLOSURE FIELD, like line 13: Section A's line 16 does not read it. The amount paid to the state only enters the arithmetic in Section B (columns (g) and (h) of line 17, then lines 19 and 23), which this module refuses. Carried so the printed schedule can be filled. The "0% rate" literal the instruction allows is a STRING entry the printed form permits in a dollar box; this fact is typed Dollar and cannot carry it, so a 0% experience-rate filer enters 0 here and the distinction is lost on the printed output - a rendering limitation with no effect on any dollar this module computes. ONE ANSWER PER SCHEDULE, like line 13: the contributions THIS filer paid. Sign: NON-NEGATIVE.

Fact.Name: Schedule H line 15, on this filer's own schedule
Fact.Description:
"Total cash wages subject to FUTA tax" (https://www.irs.gov/pub/irs-pdf/f1040sh.pdf, page 2), summed over the household employees THIS filer employed rather than over the whole return's list. Gated on this filer's own Section A routing and complete-safe to zero.
ONE OF THE COLLECTION-REACHING STEPS, so it carries the primary/secondary Switch the per-filer Section B section explains: the engine cannot Filter a collection by the CURRENT outer item, so each arm reads a NAMED per-filer collection. It is /filers/*/scheduleHLine20's body with the Section A gate substituted for the Section B one, which is the printed relationship between the two lines - line 20's own heading points back at line 15's instructions and both read the SAME total.
AN UNANSWERED EMPLOYEE COLLECTION IS NOT AN EMPTY ONE and this fact carries the explicit zero arm for the difference, ported from the twin rather than dropped. Without it, a Section A return whose /householdEmployees was never answered at all would go Placeholder here, and that Placeholder would propagate through the rollup into /knockoutScheduleHRequiredButIncomplete and silently DISARM the refusal.

Fact.Name: Schedule H line 15, the return's two schedules added
Fact.Description:
Line 15, gated on Section A and complete-safe to zero. A filer who does not reach Section A - because Part II was never entered, or because any of THEIR lines 10-12 is not an answered Yes - enters nothing HERE, which does not mean they enter nothing: the Section B filer's box is /scheduleHLine20, whose printed heading points back at these very instructions, and both read the SAME total. The two derived facts differ only in which section gates them. A filer who reaches neither section is refused by /knockoutScheduleHRequiredButIncomplete, so the zero can never be the whole story on a filed return.
This fact is a rollup over /filers/*. The Section A gate and the employee-list guard moved down to /filers/*/scheduleHLine15, which is where they now bind - once per SCHEDULE, as printed - and this fact is the sum of the two schedules' own totals. On a return with one household employer the sum IS that filer's figure, so the single-employer population is byte-identical across the change. On a two-schedule return it is no longer a single Section A base: one spouse can be in Section A while the other is in Section B, and then this fact carries only the Section A spouse's wages while /scheduleHLine20 carries only the other's.
DERIVED (not attested). Each per-filer value arm is that filer's share of /scheduleHHouseholdEmployeesLine15Total: each employee's cash wages capped at $7,000, over line 15's own SHORTER exclusion list. The retired attestation is in git history at this file.
EXPORTED, because the rebody took its last in-graph consumer. Line 16 read it, and line 16 is now a rollup over /filers/*/scheduleHLine16, each of which reads its own filer's line 15. It is a PRINTED ENTRY BOX, so an mef Export is what it was always owed - the same treatment lines 13 and 14 carry - and it is a Complete row on all 939 committed cases besides.

Fact.Name: FUTA tax, Section A, on this filer's own schedule (Schedule H line 16)
Fact.Description:
"FUTA tax. Multiply line 15 by 0.6% (0.006). Enter the result here, skip Section B, and go to line 25" (https://www.irs.gov/pub/irs-pdf/f1040sh.pdf, page 2), on THIS filer's own line 15.
ROUNDED HERE, HALF-UP, AND THAT IS THE WHOLE POINT OF THE PER-FILER PLACEMENT. Line 16 is a printed entry line on a SCHEDULE, so a return with two schedules rounds it twice. Computed once per RETURN over a line 15 that summed both spouses' employees it rounded once, and flat rates do not commute with rounding: two spouses each with $4,250 of FUTA wages give Round(25.50) = 26 twice = 52 on two printed schedules against Round(51.00) = 51 combined, a $1 UNDER-statement on the single-state, paid-on-time route. Section A applies the full credit unconditionally, which is exactly why it is gated on all three of THIS filer's lines 10, 11 and 12 being an answered Yes - those three questions ARE the conditions for the full credit, and they are asked of one schedule. Section B computes the credit line by line for everyone else (/filers/*/scheduleHLine24). Sign: NON-NEGATIVE.

Fact.Name: FUTA tax, Section A, the return's two schedules added (Schedule H line 16)
Fact.Description:
Schedule H Section A line 16: "FUTA tax. Multiply line 15 by 0.6% (0.006). Enter the result here, skip Section B, and go to line 25" (https://www.irs.gov/pub/irs-pdf/f1040sh.pdf, page 2).
This fact is a rollup over /filers/*, and it is a VALUE-MOVING change on a population that already existed. The Round moved down to /filers/*/scheduleHLine16, where it binds once per SCHEDULE as printed, and this fact is the sum of the two schedules' figures. On a return with one household employer the sum IS that filer's figure, so the single-employer population is byte-identical. ON A TWO-SCHEDULE RETURN THIS SUM IS NOT Round(0.6% x the combined line 15): each schedule rounds its own product (52 here where the merged computation gave 51).
A SECTION A FILER WHO HAS LISTED NO HOUSEHOLD EMPLOYEE IS REFUSED, by arm 2 of /knockoutScheduleHRequiredButIncomplete: line 16 would otherwise be 0.6% of a complete-safe zero and no other refusal reaches that return.
Sign: NON-NEGATIVE. The addends are already whole dollars, so this sum needs no Round of its own.

Fact.Name: The jurisdictions a Schedule H FUTA contribution row can name
Fact.Description:
The 53 jurisdictions Schedule H recognises for state unemployment contributions: the 50 states, the District of Columbia, Puerto Rico and the U.S. Virgin Islands. THE LIST IS TAKEN FROM WORKSHEET 2's OWN TABLE (https://www.irs.gov/pub/irs-pdf/i1040sh.pdf, page 9) rather than assembled by us, because that table is what the credit reduction lookup reads and a jurisdiction missing from it would have no rate. It agrees with the "State Names and Postal Abbreviations" table the line 13 instruction points at (lines 509-526).
NOT /scopedStateOptions, DELIBERATELY. That enum is the set of states this program supports for STATE-return purposes and carries a moreThanOne knockout option; it excludes Puerto Rico and the U.S. Virgin Islands, both of which Schedule H expressly names, and the Virgin Islands carries the largest credit reduction rate on the 2025 table. Reusing it would silently misroute exactly the population Worksheet 2 exists for. Federal FUTA disclosure of a state name is not state-tax scope (invariant #7).

Fact.Name: Schedule H line 17 rows - state unemployment contributions, one row per rate period
Fact.Description:
The line 17 table: "Complete all columns below that apply (if you need more space, see instructions)" (https://www.irs.gov/pub/irs-pdf/f1040sh.pdf, page 2), with columns (a) name of state, (b) taxable wages as defined in the state act, (c) state experience rate period from and to, (d) state experience rate, (e) column (b) times 0.054, (f) column (b) times column (d), (g) column (e) minus column (f) floored at zero, and (h) contributions paid to the state unemployment fund (lines 78-82).
ONE ROW PER RATE PERIOD, NOT PER STATE, and that is a printed requirement rather than a modelling choice: "If you were given a rate for only part of the year, or the rate changed during the year, you must complete a separate line for each rate period" (https://www.irs.gov/pub/irs-pdf/i1040sh.pdf, page 6). A per-state collection would be unable to represent the mid-year rate change the instruction anticipates.
THIS COLLECTION IS THE WHOLE BLOCKER THAT RETIRED. Until it existed the module refused every Section B filer (the retired /knockoutScheduleHFutaSectionB; see the module header and git history at this file). Nothing about the source was ever missing - every rate and every rule Section B needs is printed, including the 2025 credit reduction rates - so the gap was the intake shape and this fact closes it. NO INTAKE ASKS IT TODAY (SERVICE-owned, invariant #7), which is why an empty collection is the normal state and every line below is complete-safe to zero.
THE PRINTED TABLE HAS FOUR BLANK ROWS AND THIS COLLECTION IS UNBOUNDED, which is the printed instruction's own answer to the difference: "If you need more space, attach a statement using the same format as line 17" (lines 393-394). So no filer is refused for row count.

Fact.Name: Column (a) - name of state
Fact.Description:
Line 17 column (a), "Name of state" (https://www.irs.gov/pub/irs-pdf/f1040sh.pdf, page 2). Entered as the two-letter postal abbreviation, the same convention line 13 uses ("Enter the two-letter abbreviation of the name of the state (or the District of Columbia, Puerto Rico, or the U.S. Virgin Islands)", https://www.irs.gov/pub/irs-pdf/i1040sh.pdf, page 6).
TYPED Enum RATHER THAN String, unlike line 13's disclosure-only twin, because this one is READ BY ARITHMETIC: Worksheet 2 looks the jurisdiction up in its printed rate table, so a free-text entry that did not match would silently take the 0.000 arm and over-state the credit. The enum makes the lookup total.
A MISSING STATE IS REFUSED, not defaulted - see /scheduleHFutaStateContributions/*/rowIsIncomplete for the direction argument.

Fact.Name: This Schedule H state row names California
Fact.Description: Complete-safe predicate for Worksheet 2's California credit-reduction rate. It is true only when the row's state enum is answered as California, and false when the state is unanswered or names another jurisdiction.

Fact.Name: This Schedule H state row names the U.S. Virgin Islands
Fact.Description: Complete-safe predicate for Worksheet 2's U.S. Virgin Islands credit-reduction rate. It is true only when the row's state enum is answered as the Virgin Islands, and false when the state is unanswered or names another jurisdiction.

Fact.Name: Column (b) - taxable wages as defined in the state act
Fact.Description:
Line 17 column (b), "Taxable wages (as defined in state act)" (https://www.irs.gov/pub/irs-pdf/f1040sh.pdf, page 2). "Enter the taxable wages on which you must pay taxes to the unemployment fund of the state shown in column (a)" (https://www.irs.gov/pub/irs-pdf/i1040sh.pdf, page 6).
NOT THE SAME NUMBER AS LINE 20, and the difference is the whole reason Section B exists. Line 20 is the FUTA wage base (the first $7,000 of each employee's cash wages); column (b) is whatever the STATE act makes taxable, which may be larger, smaller, or drawn from a different employee set. Line 12 asks the filer directly whether the two agree, and a No there is one of the three routes into this section.
THE 0% EXPERIENCE RATE CASE IS MODELLED HERE, not lost as it is on Section A's line 14: "If your experience rate is 0%, enter the amount of wages you would have had to pay taxes on if that rate hadn't been granted" (lines 407-409). A filer granted a 0% rate enters those hypothetical wages here and 0 in column (d), which this graph distinguishes from an unanswered rate - see ../columnE. Sign: NON-NEGATIVE.

Fact.Name: Column (c) - state experience rate period, from
Fact.Description:
Line 17 column (c), "State experience rate period ... From" (https://www.irs.gov/pub/irs-pdf/f1040sh.pdf, page 2). Required of a filer given a rate: "If you were given an experience rate of 5.4% or higher, you must also complete columns (c) and (d)" (https://www.irs.gov/pub/irs-pdf/i1040sh.pdf, page 6).
A DISCLOSURE FIELD - no dollar on this schedule reads it. What does the work is the SEPARATE ROW the instruction requires per rate period; the dates say which period the row covers. Carried so the printed table can be filled and exported rather than left blank.

Fact.Name: Column (c) - state experience rate period, to
Fact.Description: Line 17 column (c), the "To" half of the rate period (https://www.irs.gov/pub/irs-pdf/f1040sh.pdf, page 2). A disclosure field on the same terms as ../writableRatePeriodFrom.

Fact.Name: Column (d) - state experience rate, in millionths
Fact.Description:
Line 17 column (d), "State experience rate" (https://www.irs.gov/pub/irs-pdf/f1040sh.pdf, page 2). "Your state will provide the experience rate. If you don't know your rate, contact your state unemployment tax agency" (https://www.irs.gov/pub/irs-pdf/i1040sh.pdf, page 6).
CARRIED AS AN Int IN MILLIONTHS OF THE DECIMAL RATE - 2.7% is 27000, 5.4% is 54000, 2.6825% is 26825 - because this dictionary has no writable Rational type and a Dollar would be a category error. The unit gives four decimal places of a percent, which covers every published state experience rate; the same Int-rate-plus-Divide shape is already shipping at form8396:/writableMccCreditRatePercent, whose divisor is 100 rather than 1,000,000. ../columnF divides the product back down.
AN ANSWERED 0 IS NOT THE SAME AS AN UNANSWERED RATE, and this is the distinction the printed instruction turns on. "You must complete columns (a), (b), and (h), EVEN IF you weren't given an experience rate" (lines 396-398): a filer with no rate at all completes neither (c) nor (d) and earns no additional credit, so ../columnE, ../columnF and ../columnG are all zero for them. A filer GRANTED a 0% rate has a rate; they enter 0 here and the hypothetical wages in column (b), and column (g) gives them the full 5.4% additional credit that the grant was worth. Section A's line 14 cannot express that case at all (its "0% rate" string literal does not fit a Dollar box) - here it is exact. Sign: NON-NEGATIVE.

Fact.Name: Column (h) - contributions paid to the state unemployment fund
Fact.Description:
Line 17 column (h), "Contributions paid to state unemployment fund" (https://www.irs.gov/pub/irs-pdf/f1040sh.pdf, page 2).
ON-TIME CONTRIBUTIONS ONLY, and this is the single most load-bearing reading in Section B: "Enter the total contributions (defined earlier) you paid to the state unemployment fund for 2025 BY APRIL 15, 2026" (https://www.irs.gov/pub/irs-pdf/i1040sh.pdf, page 6). Anything paid after that date is excluded here and re-enters through Worksheet 1 at 90% (/scheduleHFutaWorksheet1Line4). Worksheet 1 line 7's "Add lines 2 and 6" is only coherent on this reading - line 2 is line 19, which is built from this column, and the worksheet ADDS the discounted late contributions to it rather than discounting a total that already contained them.
NOT ROUNDED PER ROW, unlike columns (e) and (f), and the asymmetry is deliberate. The rounding convention rounds PRODUCTS at their printed line; columns (e) and (f) are products this graph computes, but column (h) is an amount the filer WROTE DOWN and may write in cents. Rounding it per row would move the filer's own figure; line 18 rounds the column total once instead, which is where the printed form asks for a total.
Sign: NON-NEGATIVE. Contributions exclude "any payments deducted or deductible from your employees' pay", penalties, interest, special administrative taxes and voluntary contributions paid to get a lower rate (lines 391-400) - definitional guidance that shapes the number the filer enters, with no separate box on the printed form.

Fact.Name: Worksheet 2 - FUTA taxable wages for this jurisdiction
Fact.Description:
Worksheet 2 line 3's "FUTA Taxable Wages" box for the state this row names: "For each state with a credit reduction rate greater than zero, enter the FUTA taxable wages, multiply by the reduction rate, and then enter the credit reduction amount" (https://www.irs.gov/pub/irs-pdf/i1040sh.pdf, page 9).
A THIRD WAGE FIGURE, DISTINCT FROM BOTH COLUMN (b) AND LINE 20, and the worksheet says so twice in one breath: "Don't enter your state unemployment wages in the FUTA Taxable Wages box. Also don't include in the FUTA Taxable Wages box wages that were excluded from state unemployment tax" (lines 557-559). So it is neither column (b) (which IS the state unemployment wages) nor line 20 (which is the whole return's FUTA base across every jurisdiction). It is the part of the FUTA base attributable to THIS jurisdiction. Nothing in the graph can derive it, so it is intake.
ONLY READ ON A CREDIT REDUCTION ROW. Every 2025 jurisdiction except California and the U.S. Virgin Islands has a reduction rate of 0.000, so on every other row this figure multiplies to nothing and is not required. On a CA or VI row it is required, because an unanswered value would compute a zero reduction and UNDER-state the tax - see ../rowIsIncomplete. Sign: NON-NEGATIVE.
PER ROW, WHILE THE PRINTED BOX IS PER STATE. A jurisdiction split across two rate periods has two rows here and one box on the worksheet; the reduction is computed distributively and summed, which is the same total (see /scheduleHFutaWorksheet2Line4 for the rounding consequence). The filer's obligation not to count the same wages twice is the same obligation the printed single box carries.

Fact.Name: Which filer's Schedule H this line 17 row belongs to
Fact.Description:
The employer attribution on the line 17 table, the second half of the per-filer dimension whose employee half landed with the collection itself. "Only two Schedules H can be attached to Form 1040, 1040-SR, and 1040-SS, one Schedule H for each of the primary taxpayer and the secondary taxpayer" (https://www.irs.gov/pub/irs-pdf/i1040sh.pdf, page 4), and line 17 is a table on a SCHEDULE - so on an MFJ return each state contribution row sits on one spouse's table, not on the return's.
WHY THE ROW AND NOT THE STATE. A jurisdiction is not the discriminator: both spouses can pay the same state, and the printed instruction already makes the row's grain a rate PERIOD rather than a state ("If you were given a rate for only part of the year, or the rate changed during the year, you must complete a separate line for each rate period", lines 402-405). Two spouses with their own experience rates in the same state are two rows, and this fact is what keeps their columns (g) and (h) on their own line 18 totals.
UNANSWERED IS THE PRIMARY FILER, exactly as ../../householdEmployees/*/writableEmployerFiler reads it, and for the same reason: one household employer means one schedule and the attribution question is never asked. That default is what keeps the single-employer population byte-identical across this fill.

Fact.Name: This row names a 2025 credit reduction jurisdiction
Fact.Description:
Whether column (a) names a jurisdiction whose Worksheet 2 reduction rate is greater than zero. For 2025 that is California (0.012) and the U.S. Virgin Islands (0.045); every other jurisdiction on the printed table is 0.000 (https://www.irs.gov/pub/irs-pdf/i1040sh.pdf, page 9).
"You're in a credit reduction state if you're a household employer in a state which has an amount greater than zero in the 'Reduction Rate' column of Worksheet 2" (lines 447-450) - the printed definition, read off the printed table rather than from any outside list. Complete-safe to false on an unanswered state, with the row-level refusal (../rowIsIncomplete) rather than this fact carrying the safety.

Fact.Name: Column (e) - column (b) multiplied by 0.054
Fact.Description:
Line 17 column (e), "Multiply col. (b) by 0.054" (https://www.irs.gov/pub/irs-pdf/f1040sh.pdf, page 2). 0.054 is the maximum state credit rate the FUTA statute allows (https://www.irs.gov/pub/irs-pdf/i1040sh.pdf, page 6), so column (e) is what the filer WOULD have been charged by the state at the full credit rate.
ZERO WHEN NO EXPERIENCE RATE WAS GIVEN, which is the printed routing and not a safety wrapper: "You must complete columns (a), (b), and (h), even if you weren't given an experience rate" (lines 396-398). Columns (e), (f) and (g) exist to give ADDITIONAL credit for the gap between the filer's own experience rate and 5.4%; with no rate there is no gap to compute, and the filer's credit is column (h) alone. Reading an unanswered rate as zero instead would hand that filer the entire 5.4% as additional credit and UNDER-state the tax by the whole amount - the one arm in this section where a complete-safe zero would have been the dangerous choice.
ROUNDED HERE, HALF-UP, because column (e) is a printed box carrying a product, and because this collection's rows ARE the printed table's rows - one per rate period - so rounding per row is exactly what a paper filer does.

Fact.Name: Column (f) - column (b) multiplied by column (d)
Fact.Description:
Line 17 column (f), "Multiply col. (b) by col. (d)" (https://www.irs.gov/pub/irs-pdf/f1040sh.pdf, page 2): the contributions the state's own experience rate would have charged on the state-taxable wages.
THE RATE IS DIVIDED BACK OUT OF ITS MILLIONTHS ENCODING here (see ../writableStateExperienceRate). The product is formed in cents and divided by 1,000,000 before the Round, so the intermediate is cent-precise rather than pre-rounded - the same Int-rate shape form8396:/form8396TentativeCredit uses with a divisor of 100.
SAME NO-RATE GATE AS COLUMN (e), and it must be the same gate: an unanswered rate reaching this multiplication as zero would make column (f) zero while column (e) stayed at 5.4%, producing the maximum additional credit for a filer entitled to none.
ROUNDED HERE, HALF-UP, as a printed box carrying a product.

Fact.Name: Column (g) - column (e) minus column (f), floored at zero
Fact.Description:
Line 17 column (g), "Subtract col. (f) from col. (e). If zero or less, enter -0-" (https://www.irs.gov/pub/irs-pdf/f1040sh.pdf, page 2). The ADDITIONAL CREDIT: the amount by which a below-5.4% experience rate reduced what the state charged, which the FUTA credit gives back.
THE FLOOR IS PRINTED, not inferred, and it binds on every row whose experience rate is 5.4% or higher - the population the instruction sends here without requiring column (e)'s companion columns at all. At a column (g) rate of 5.39% the additional credit is a positive dollar; at 5.41% the floor binds and the credit is zero.
Both operands are already whole dollars, so no Round is needed here.

Fact.Name: Column (h) as entered, complete-safe
Fact.Description:
The contributions-paid entry with unanswered read as zero. Carried in CENTS rather than rounded per row - see ../writableContributionsPaid for why this column is treated differently from the two product columns.
AN UNANSWERED COLUMN (h) IS NOT REFUSED. It resolves to zero, which reduces line 19 and therefore the credit, and so OVER-states the tax. The module refuses the under-stating direction only (see /knockoutScheduleHRequiredButIncomplete); a filer who omits their own contributions pays more, not less, and nothing in the return can adjudicate the omission.

Fact.Name: Worksheet 2 - this row's credit reduction amount
Fact.Description:
The row's contribution to Worksheet 2 line 4: FUTA taxable wages for the jurisdiction multiplied by its printed 2025 reduction rate. CALIFORNIA 0.012, U.S. VIRGIN ISLANDS 0.045, every other jurisdiction 0.000 (https://www.irs.gov/pub/irs-pdf/i1040sh.pdf, page 9).
THE RATES ARE PRINTED AND THAT IS WHY THIS EXISTS. The refusal this section retires never rested on a missing rate table - it rested on having no per-state wage figure to multiply by. Both rates are quoted from the Worksheet 2 table itself; the 0.000 arm is every other jurisdiction on that same table, so the Switch is total over the enum.
CENT-PRECISE, NOT ROUNDED HERE. The printed Credit Reduction box is per STATE while these rows are per RATE PERIOD, so this value is not itself a printed box; the rounding happens once at /scheduleHFutaWorksheet2Line4. For the printed shape (one row per state) the two are identical.

Fact.Name: This line 17 row is on the primary filer's Schedule H
Fact.Description: The primary half of the line 17 attribution, built to the same shape /householdEmployees/*/belongsToPrimaryFiler uses (which is in turn formW2s:/formW2s/*/belongsToPrimaryFiler's). AN UNANSWERED ../writableEmployerFiler counts as the primary filer, so a single-employer return never sees the question and its rows all land on the one schedule it files.

Fact.Name: This line 17 row is on the secondary filer's Schedule H
Fact.Description: The secondary half of the line 17 attribution. It requires an ANSWERED ../writableEmployerFiler, the mirror of ../belongsToPrimaryFiler's default, so that every row belongs to exactly one filer and no column (h) is either dropped or double-counted by the two named collections below.

Fact.Name: This row is missing an answer the graph cannot safely default
Fact.Description:
The per-row half of the Part II completeness guard. TWO CLAUSES, AND BOTH ARE HERE FOR THE SAME REASON - each would otherwise UNDER-state the tax:
(1) NO STATE NAMED. Column (a) is required of every row ("You must complete columns (a), (b), and (h)", https://www.irs.gov/pub/irs-pdf/i1040sh.pdf, page 6), but the reason this graph refuses rather than defaults is narrower and worth stating exactly: an unnamed jurisdiction could be California or the U.S. Virgin Islands, and ../creditReduction would silently take its 0.000 arm and hand back a credit the filer is not entitled to.
(2) A CREDIT REDUCTION ROW WITH NO FUTA TAXABLE WAGES. On a CA or VI row an unanswered ../writableFutaTaxableWages computes a zero reduction, which is the same under-statement by a different route.
COLUMNS (b) AND (h) ARE DELIBERATELY NOT HERE even though the same sentence requires them, and the asymmetry is the module's stated policy rather than an oversight: a missing column (b) zeroes columns (e) through (g) and a missing column (h) zeroes that row's credit, so each OVER-states the tax. This module refuses the under-stating direction only (module header; /knockoutScheduleHRequiredButIncomplete). Adding an over-stating refusal would be new policy, not a bug fix.
Likewise the EXPERIENCE RATE is absent from this list on purpose - an unanswered rate is a printed, legitimate state ("even if you weren't given an experience rate") and ../columnE handles it safely.

Fact.Name: Line 17 rows missing an answer the graph cannot safely default
Fact.Description: The subset of /scheduleHFutaStateContributions whose ../rowIsIncomplete is true. A filter rather than a count so the application surface can point the filer at the rows that need finishing.

Fact.Name: At least one line 17 row is unfinished
Fact.Description: Whether /scheduleHFutaIncompleteRows is non-empty. The predicate /scheduleHPartIIAnswersAreComplete negates.

Fact.Name: Line 17 rows on the primary filer's Schedule H
Fact.Description:
The primary filer's share of /scheduleHFutaStateContributions, built to the shape /primaryFilerHouseholdEmployees uses.
WHY A NAMED COLLECTION RATHER THAN A FILTER UNDER /filers/*. This is the structural fact the per-filer chain is built around: the engine cannot Filter a collection by the CURRENT outer item - a Filter binds the filtered collection's own row context and cannot close over the /filers/* item it sits under. So every per-filer step that reaches this table (the two line 18 totals and Worksheet 2 line 4) carries a Switch on ../isPrimaryFiler against ../isSecondaryFiler and reads one of these two NAMED collections on each arm. Purely arithmetic per-filer steps need no such pair and are one fact each.

Fact.Name: Line 17 rows on the secondary filer's Schedule H
Fact.Description: The secondary filer's share of /scheduleHFutaStateContributions, built to the shape /secondaryFilerHouseholdEmployees uses. See /primaryFilerScheduleHFutaStateContributions for why the per-filer chain needs a NAMED pair rather than a Filter under /filers/*.

Fact.Name: Line 17 rows on this filer's own Schedule H
Fact.Description:
The line 17 rows this filer's own printed Schedule H lists: the primary filer's rows (/primaryFilerScheduleHFutaStateContributions) on the primary filer's copy, the secondary filer's rows (/secondaryFilerScheduleHFutaStateContributions) on the secondary filer's copy. "Only two Schedules H can be attached to Form 1040, 1040-SR, and 1040-SS, one Schedule H for each of the primary taxpayer and the secondary taxpayer", so each spouse's line 17 lists the states that spouse paid.
A SWITCH BETWEEN THE TWO NAMED FILTERS, NOT A FILTER UNDER /filers/*. A Filter binds the filtered collection's own row context and cannot close over the filer it sits under; both named Filters stand for /scheduleHFutaStateContributions, so choosing between them by this filer's role is legal and keeps every row's identity. The printed form's line 17 boxes and the continuation statement read this collection by position on each filer's copy.
A filer whose role cannot be read lists the primary filer's rows: that is the one printed schedule a return with one employer carries, and it is where an unattributed row belongs by /scheduleHFutaStateContributions/*/belongsToPrimaryFiler's own default. No dollar reads it; the per-filer line 18 totals read the named Filters directly.

Fact.Name: Schedule H line 18, column (g) total
Fact.Description:
Line 18: "Totals" (https://www.irs.gov/pub/irs-pdf/f1040sh.pdf, page 2). "Add the amounts in columns (g) and (h) SEPARATELY and enter the totals in the spaces provided" (https://www.irs.gov/pub/irs-pdf/i1040sh.pdf, page 7) - two totals, which is why this fact and /scheduleHLine18ColumnHTotal are separate rather than one sum.
GATED ON SECTION B and complete-safe to zero, the same shape /scheduleHLine15 uses for Section A. A return that never reaches Section B carries no line 17 rows and totals nothing; a return that reaches Section A but has stray rows still totals nothing here, because the printed form sends it past this table entirely ("Enter the result here, skip Section B, and go to line 25", line 75).
This fact is a rollup over /filers/*. The Section B gate, the Round and the column-(g)-only reading all moved down to /filers/*/scheduleHLine18ColumnGTotal, which is where they now bind - once per SCHEDULE, as printed. This fact is the sum of the two schedules' own totals. On a return with one household employer the sum is that filer's own figure, so the single-employer population is byte-identical across the change.

Fact.Name: Schedule H line 18, column (h) total
Fact.Description:
The second of line 18's two printed totals (see /scheduleHLine18ColumnGTotal).
THIS IS WHERE COLUMN (h) ROUNDS. Each row's column (h) is the filer's own entered amount and may carry cents; the printed form asks for a total here, so the cents are added first and the sum rounds once. For example, 270.50 + 270.49 totals 540.99 and enters line 19 as 541.
This fact is a rollup over /filers/*. The computation moved down to /filers/*/scheduleHLine18ColumnHTotal, where it now binds once per SCHEDULE as printed, and this fact is the sum of the two schedules' own figures. On a return with one household employer the sum IS that filer's figure, so the single-employer population is byte-identical across the change.

Fact.Name: Schedule H line 19 - total state unemployment credit before the two limits
Fact.Description:
Line 19: "Add columns (g) and (h) of line 18" (https://www.irs.gov/pub/irs-pdf/f1040sh.pdf, page 2), restated at https://www.irs.gov/pub/irs-pdf/i1040sh.pdf, page 7.
WHAT IT MEANS: the filer's total state unemployment credit - the additional credit for a below-5.4% experience rate plus the contributions they actually paid ON TIME. Late contributions are NOT in it (see /scheduleHFutaStateContributions/*/writableContributionsPaid); they reach the credit through Worksheet 1 at 90%.
This fact is a rollup over /filers/*. The computation moved down to /filers/*/scheduleHLine19, where it now binds once per SCHEDULE as printed, and this fact is the sum of the two schedules' own figures. On a return with one household employer the sum IS that filer's figure, so the single-employer population is byte-identical across the change.

Fact.Name: Schedule H line 20 - total cash wages subject to FUTA tax
Fact.Description:
Line 20: "Total cash wages subject to FUTA tax (see the line 15 instructions)" (https://www.irs.gov/pub/irs-pdf/f1040sh.pdf, page 2). The instruction is explicit that this is the same quantity line 15 defines: "Enter the total cash wages subject to FUTA tax. See the instructions for line 15, earlier" (https://www.irs.gov/pub/irs-pdf/i1040sh.pdf, page 7).
ONE TOTAL SERVES BOTH BOXES, exactly as lines C and 9 share /writableScheduleHPaidCashWages1000OrMoreInAnyQuarter. Lines 15 and 20 are the same question asked on two mutually exclusive routes - line 15 of the Section A filer, line 20 of the Section B filer - and a single quantity cannot disagree with itself. That quantity is /scheduleHHouseholdEmployeesLine15Total, a derivation from the employee collection rather than the retired attestation; the two DERIVED facts still differ only in which section gates them.
GATED ON SECTION B and on the employee list carrying the wages. An empty collection makes lines 21 and 22 zero and line 24 zero, which is why /knockoutScheduleHRequiredButIncomplete refuses that return rather than filing it - see /scheduleHPartIIAnswersAreComplete arm 3, which had to be rewritten against the collection in the same landing.
This fact is a rollup over /filers/*. The computation moved down to /filers/*/scheduleHLine20, where it now binds once per SCHEDULE as printed, and this fact is the sum of the two schedules' own figures. On a return with one household employer the sum IS that filer's figure, so the single-employer population is byte-identical across the change.

Fact.Name: Schedule H line 21 - gross FUTA tax at 6.0%
Fact.Description:
Line 21: "Multiply line 20 by 6.0% (0.06)" (https://www.irs.gov/pub/irs-pdf/f1040sh.pdf, page 2). "The FUTA tax rate is 6.0% for 2025" (https://www.irs.gov/pub/irs-pdf/i1040sh.pdf, page 6).
THE GROSS RATE, before any state credit - the figure Section A never computes because Section A goes straight to the 0.6% net rate. Rounded here, HALF-UP, as a printed entry line. Sign: NON-NEGATIVE.
This fact is a rollup over /filers/*. The computation moved down to /filers/*/scheduleHLine21, where it now binds once per SCHEDULE as printed, and this fact is the sum of the two schedules' own figures. On a return with one household employer the sum IS that filer's figure, so the single-employer population is byte-identical across the change. ON A TWO-SCHEDULE RETURN THIS SUM IS NOT Round(6.0% x the combined line 20): each schedule rounds its own product (502 here where the merged computation gave 501).

Fact.Name: Schedule H line 22 - the maximum state credit at 5.4%
Fact.Description:
Line 22: "Multiply line 20 by 5.4% (0.054)" (https://www.irs.gov/pub/irs-pdf/f1040sh.pdf, page 2). The statutory ceiling on the state credit: "You may be able to take a credit of up to 5.4% against the FUTA tax, resulting in a net FUTA tax rate of 0.6%" (https://www.irs.gov/pub/irs-pdf/i1040sh.pdf, page 6).
THIS IS WHY LINE 24 CAN NEVER BE NEGATIVE. Line 23 is capped at line 22, and line 22 is 5.4% of the same base line 21 takes 6.0% of, so line 21 minus line 23 is at least 0.6% of line 20 for any non-negative line 20. Rounded here, HALF-UP, as a printed entry line.
This fact is a rollup over /filers/*. The computation moved down to /filers/*/scheduleHLine22, where it now binds once per SCHEDULE as printed, and this fact is the sum of the two schedules' own figures. On a return with one household employer the sum IS that filer's figure, so the single-employer population is byte-identical across the change. THE CAP STOPS BEING SHARED HERE, which is the whole unit: each schedule's ceiling is 5.4% of ITS OWN line 20 and line 23 caps against that, so one spouse's clipped credit can no longer reach the other's headroom. The rounding also moves per schedule (450 here where the merged computation gave 451).

Fact.Name: Worksheet 1 line 1 - the amount from Schedule H line 22
Fact.Description:
"Enter the amount from Schedule H, line 22" (https://www.irs.gov/pub/irs-pdf/i1040sh.pdf, page 8): the 5.4% ceiling on the whole credit. Carried as its own fact rather than inlined so the worksheet reads against the printed page line for line, the same convention the module uses for the schedule itself.
This fact is a rollup over /filers/*. The computation moved down to /filers/*/scheduleHFutaWorksheet1Line1, where it now binds once per SCHEDULE as printed, and this fact is the sum of the two schedules' own figures. On a return with one household employer the sum IS that filer's figure, so the single-employer population is byte-identical across the change.

Fact.Name: Worksheet 1 line 2 - the amount from Schedule H line 19
Fact.Description:
"Enter the amount from Schedule H, line 19" (https://www.irs.gov/pub/irs-pdf/i1040sh.pdf, page 8): the credit earned from the additional credit and the ON-TIME contributions.
This fact is a rollup over /filers/*. The computation moved down to /filers/*/scheduleHFutaWorksheet1Line2, where it now binds once per SCHEDULE as printed, and this fact is the sum of the two schedules' own figures. On a return with one household employer the sum IS that filer's figure, so the single-employer population is byte-identical across the change.

Fact.Name: Worksheet 1 line 3 - headroom under the 5.4% ceiling
Fact.Description:
"Subtract line 2 from line 1. If zero or less, enter -0-" (https://www.irs.gov/pub/irs-pdf/i1040sh.pdf, page 8). How much credit the filer could still earn before hitting the statutory ceiling - and therefore the most their late contributions can be worth.
This fact is a rollup over /filers/*. The computation moved down to /filers/*/scheduleHFutaWorksheet1Line3, where it now binds once per SCHEDULE as printed, and this fact is the sum of the two schedules' own figures. On a return with one household employer the sum IS that filer's figure, so the single-employer population is byte-identical across the change. The rollup keeps each spouse's own floored line 3: where the primary spouse overpaid (a negative headroom) and the secondary spouse's is 278, the result is 278, whereas netting them on a merged schedule would give 156.

Fact.Name: Worksheet 1 line 4 - late contributions, complete-safe
Fact.Description: The late-contributions figure the return carries, as the sum of the two schedules' own complete-safe line 4s. See /filers/*/writableScheduleHFutaContributionsPaidAfterDueDate for why a zero forfeits credit and over-states the tax, and is therefore safe to default; the return-level writable this fact used to alias is retired (see the note above /scheduleHFutaWorksheet1Line1).

Fact.Name: Worksheet 1 line 5 - late contributions that fit under the ceiling
Fact.Description:
"Enter the smaller of line 3 or line 4" (https://www.irs.gov/pub/irs-pdf/i1040sh.pdf, page 8). Late contributions beyond the headroom earn nothing, because the total credit is capped at 5.4% either way.
This fact is a rollup over /filers/*. The computation moved down to /filers/*/scheduleHFutaWorksheet1Line5, where it now binds once per SCHEDULE as printed, and this fact is the sum of the two schedules' own figures. On a return with one household employer the sum IS that filer's figure, so the single-employer population is byte-identical across the change.

Fact.Name: Worksheet 1 line 6 - the 90% limit on late contributions
Fact.Description:
"Multiply line 5 by 90% (0.90)" (https://www.irs.gov/pub/irs-pdf/i1040sh.pdf, page 8). THE PENALTY THIS WORKSHEET EXISTS FOR: "The credit you can take for any state unemployment fund contributions for 2025 that you pay after April 15, 2026, is limited to 90% of the credit that would have been allowable if the contributions were paid on or before April 15, 2026" (lines 386-390).
The haircut is 10% of the late contributions, not of the whole credit - line 7 adds this to line 2 rather than replacing it. Rounded here, HALF-UP, as the worksheet's own printed box and the only product in Worksheet 1. Sign: NON-NEGATIVE.
This fact is a rollup over /filers/*. The computation moved down to /filers/*/scheduleHFutaWorksheet1Line6, where it now binds once per SCHEDULE as printed, and this fact is the sum of the two schedules' own figures. On a return with one household employer the sum IS that filer's figure, so the single-employer population is byte-identical across the change.

Fact.Name: Worksheet 1 line 7 - on-time credit plus the discounted late credit
Fact.Description:
"Add lines 2 and 6" (https://www.irs.gov/pub/irs-pdf/i1040sh.pdf, page 8).

Fact.Name: Schedule H line 22, on this filer's own schedule - THE CAP THIS UNIT UNSHARES

Fact.Name: This filer's own Schedule H reaches Part II with their own lines 10-12 unanswered
Fact.Description:
The per-filer half of the Part II completeness guard, built when the routing questions became per filer. It answers "does THIS filer have a schedule that reaches Part II and has answered neither routing question set?" - not "did somebody on the return answer", which is what the return-level predicate could ask and is the reason the guard had to be rewritten rather than ported.
WHO REACHES PART II, and this is the reading the fact turns on. A filer reaches Part II when the return does (/scheduleHFutaApplies - the $1,000-quarter test, which lines C and 9 ask about all the return's household employees at once) AND that filer actually employs a household employee, because "Only two Schedules H can be attached ... one Schedule H for each of the primary taxpayer and the secondary taxpayer" (https://www.irs.gov/pub/irs-pdf/i1040sh.pdf, page 4) means a filer who employs nobody has no schedule to answer lines 10-12 on. Requiring an answer from them would refuse the commonest MFJ return in the corpus - one household employer, a spouse who employs no one - over a box the printed form never puts in front of them. interpretation:provisional.
THE EMPLOYEE LIST IS THE EMPLOYER TEST, not the line 17 table, and the asymmetry is deliberate. A filer with line 17 rows but no employees has a line 20 of zero, so their Section B tax is zero and ignoring their rows OVER-states rather than under-states - the direction this module does not refuse.
ONE OF THE COLLECTION-REACHING FACTS, so it carries the primary/secondary Switch, and every arm is guarded: an unanswered /householdEmployees takes the explicit false arm rather than counting an unanswered collection as empty.
IT WIDENS A REFUSAL, AND THE CONTRACT THAT ASKED FOR IT SAID IT WOULD NOT. The population is exactly one shape: an MFJ return where BOTH spouses employ household staff and only ONE of them has answered lines 10-12. Before the split there was a single return-level answer set covering both schedules, so a filled-in primary carried the secondary along and the return filed at 0.6% of both spouses' wages; now the unanswered spouse reaches neither section and /knockoutScheduleHRequiredButIncomplete fires. That is the module's standing direction rather than a new policy - Section A produces the LOWEST FUTA figure the schedule can, and this return's second schedule genuinely has no routing answer - but the contract's clause "NO REFUSAL RETIRES OR ARRIVES WITH THIS ONE" is FALSE as written, and this module's convention is that a new refusal population is WITNESSED rather than discovered later.

Fact.Name: Filers whose own Schedule H reaches Part II unanswered
Fact.Description: The subset of /filers whose ../scheduleHPartIIAnswersAreIncomplete is true. A filter rather than a count so the application surface can point the filer at the schedule that needs finishing, the same reason /scheduleHFutaIncompleteRows is one.

Fact.Name: At least one filer's Schedule H reaches Part II unanswered
Fact.Description:
Whether /filersWithIncompleteScheduleHPartIIAnswers is non-empty - the predicate /scheduleHPartIIAnswersAreComplete negates. It replaces the return-level "neither section applies" residue test the guard used to carry inline, which could only ask whether SOMEBODY answered.
THE IsComplete(/filers) GUARD WITH AN EXPLICIT FALSE ARM: a Filter over an unanswered collection resolves Placeholder, and a Placeholder here would have propagated into /knockoutScheduleHRequiredButIncomplete, which every return in the corpus resolves. FALSE is the non-refusing arm, so the guard never refuses a return it cannot measure.

Fact.Name: Every Part II line the routing requires has been answered, on every schedule the return carries
Fact.Description:
The Part II counterpart of /scheduleHPartIAnswersAreComplete, and the predicate arm 2 of /knockoutScheduleHRequiredButIncomplete negates.
REWRITTEN FOR THE ROUTING BEING PER FILER. Its arms 2 and 3 used to read the return-level routing predicates, one per printed section, and that shape cannot express the requirement any more: "somebody answered lines 10-12" is satisfied by ONE spouse on a two-schedule return, leaving the other's schedule unanswered and unrefused. The requirement is now "every filer who reaches Part II has answered their own three", carried by /scheduleHSomeFilerHasIncompletePartIIAnswers, and the two printed section arms collapse into one because they always required the SAME employee list.
TWO ARMS NOW:
(1) PART II NOT ENTERED. The $1,000-quarter question is not a Yes, so lines 10 through 24 are all skipped and nothing is owed.
(2) PART II ENTERED AND EVERY SCHEDULE FINISHED. The household employee list - which lines 15 and 20 are both summed from - must be non-empty and finished, no filer may reach Part II with their own lines 10-12 unanswered, and IF any schedule on the return reaches Section B, every line 17 row must be finished to the extent the graph cannot safely default it (/scheduleHFutaStateContributions/*/rowIsIncomplete). The line 17 requirement is conditional because a return whose only schedule is a Section A one has no line 17 table to finish.
THE RESIDUE IS REFUSED, WHICH IS THE POINT, and it is now refused per schedule. A filer who employs household staff and has answered NONE of their own lines 10-12 reaches neither Section A nor Section B, so their arm of /filers/*/scheduleHPartIIAnswersAreIncomplete is true and the guard fires - even when their spouse answered all three. That preserves the direction the retired /knockoutScheduleHFutaSectionB was built around: Section A produces the lowest FUTA figure the schedule can, so an unanswered routing question must never default into it.
THE EMPLOYEE-LIST PAIR IS UNCHANGED from the rewrite that introduced it (/scheduleHHouseholdEmployeesListed and /scheduleHHouseholdEmployeesHaveIncompleteRow): the totals are CollectionSums, which are Complete at zero over an empty collection, so an IsComplete test on them would pass vacuously and let both FUTA routes file zero unrefused.

Fact.Name: Schedule H line 25
Fact.Description:

If you checked the 'Yes' box on line C of page 1, enter -0-" (https://www.irs.gov/pub/irs-pdf/f1040sh.pdf, page 2), with the instruction adding "If there is no entry on line 8, enter -0-" (https://www.irs.gov/pub/irs-pdf/i1040sh.pdf, page 7).
THE LINE-C ARM IS MODELLED EXPLICITLY EVEN THOUGH IT IS ARITHMETICALLY REDUNDANT HERE, and that is deliberate. Line C is REACHED only after No on line A and No on line B, and on that route /scheduleHLine1, /scheduleHLine3, /scheduleHLine5 and /scheduleHLine7 are all zero by their own gating, so line 8 is already zero and both arms agree. Writing the printed condition anyway keeps this fact readable against the form and keeps the two gatings independent: if a later unit ever loosens a Part I gate, this line still obeys the printed rule rather than silently inheriting a Part I change.

Fact.Name: This schedule's FUTA tax - Part III line 26's "line 16 (or line 24)" for one filer
Fact.Description:
The FUTA half of Part III line 26, "Add line 16 (or line 24) and line 25" (https://www.irs.gov/pub/irs-pdf/f1040sh.pdf, page 2), on THIS filer's own schedule.
THE PRINTED "OR" IS EXCLUSIVE PER SCHEDULE, AND THAT IS THE ONLY LEVEL IT HOLDS AT. Each schedule reaches exactly one section - ../scheduleHFutaSectionAApplies and ../scheduleHFutaSectionBApplies cannot both be true for one filer, the second being gated on Not the first - so at most one of this filer's lines 16 and 24 is nonzero and the Add selects the same number the printed "or" does. What is NEW is that the exclusion is no longer true of the RETURN: one spouse can file Section A while the other files Section B, which is the population the routing split exists for, and the return-level /scheduleHLine16 and /scheduleHLine24 are then BOTH nonzero at once. DECLARED SO THE COMBINATION IS READABLE. /scheduleHTotalHouseholdEmploymentTaxes still adds the two return-level rollups rather than a rollup of this fact: both routes give the same number, and rewiring an exported fact's dependency shape for no dollar would be churn. So this fact is EXPORTED rather than consumed, and that is honest rather than a lint dodge - the thing that needs one FUTA figure per schedule is the application surface that prints the two schedules (invariant #7), which is the same reason /scheduleHReturnHasTwoHouseholdEmployers is exported. Sign: NON-NEGATIVE. Both addends are already whole dollars.

Fact.Name: Total household employment taxes (Schedule H line 26, to Schedule 2 line 9)
Fact.Description:
Schedule H Part III line 26: "Add line 16 (or line 24) and line 25" (https://www.irs.gov/pub/irs-pdf/f1040sh.pdf, page 2).
THE PRINTED "OR" IS AN EXCLUSIVE ONE AND THIS Add RELIES ON IT - BUT THE EXCLUSION HOLDS PER SCHEDULE, NOT PER RETURN, and that is the sentence a reader must not skim. Line 16 is Section A's FUTA tax and line 24 is Section B's, and each SCHEDULE reaches exactly one section: /filers/*/scheduleHFutaSectionAApplies and /filers/*/scheduleHFutaSectionBApplies cannot both be true for one filer, and whichever line the filer's schedule skips is gated to zero by its own Switch (/filers/*/scheduleHLine15 on the first, /filers/*/scheduleHLine20 and the line 18 totals on the second). Both return-level rollups can now be nonzero AT ONCE, on an MFJ return whose two spouses route differently, and adding them is exactly right for that return - it is the two printed schedules' "line 16 (or line 24)" added, which is what /filers/*/scheduleHFutaTax names one filer's half of. Adding all three addends is therefore still the number the printed "or" selects, without a Switch that would have to re-derive the routing a third time. THIS IS SCHEDULE 2 LINE 9. Line 27's chart routes it: "IF you file Form 1040 or 1040-SR ... THEN enter the amount from Schedule H, line 8 or, if applicable, line 26, on Schedule 2 (Form 1040), line 9" (https://www.irs.gov/pub/irs-pdf/i1040sh.pdf, page 7), and the form repeats it at line 27 ("Yes. Stop. Include the amount from line 26 above on Schedule 2 (Form 1040), line 9", line 101). The chart's "line 8 or, if applicable, line 26" is not a choice between two different numbers: line 26 is defined for every filer who reaches Part III, and equals line 25 (= line 8) plus whichever of lines 16 and 24 the filer's own Part II routing reached. So routing line 26 unconditionally is the same number the chart names, and it is what line 27's own Yes branch says. ("a line 16 ... plus a line 24" here: both are zero for anyone who never entered Part II, and at most one is nonzero for anyone who did.)
ZERO ON EVERY RETURN THAT ANSWERS NOTHING, which is what makes this module additive: the wiring into taxCalculations /line21OfSchedule2 changes no committed scenario's total tax. Sign: NON-NEGATIVE. Rounded here as a printed entry line, a no-op over two whole-dollar addends.

Fact.Name: Refusal for a Schedule H filer who has not supplied the entries their own answers require
Fact.Description:
Refuses the filer who has not finished the schedule their own answers put in front of them. TWO ARMS, one per Part, and arm 2 is widened to cover Section B - it used to name Section A's line 15 only.
ARM 1 - PART I. The filer answered Yes to line A or line B and has not supplied every Part I entry that answer puts in front of them (see /scheduleHPartIAnswersAreComplete for the printed routing this negates). WIDENED AGAIN for lines 1, 3 and 5 becoming derivations: on the line-A path the arm now also fires when the employee list holds NOBODY line A's Yes could be about (/scheduleHHouseholdEmployeesSupportLineA) or holds a row whose unanswered fields would exclude someone who should count (/householdEmployees/*/rowIsIncomplete). The first of those is a NEW refusal population - a filer who checked Yes on line A and listed no employee at or above $2,800 could file at $0 before this landing, by answering the four retired attestations with zeros. Line A's own instruction applies the same exclusion list the collection does, so the Yes and the list cannot honestly disagree; the direction is the module's standing one, since every arm of that disagreement UNDER-states.
ARM 2 - PART II, ALL ROUTES. The predicate is /scheduleHPartIIAnswersAreComplete, which carries the three printed routes: Part II never entered (nothing owed), Section A (line 15 required), and Section B (line 20 required, plus every line 17 row finished to the extent the graph cannot safely default it). It ALSO catches the residue that belongs to no route - the Part II filer who has answered NONE of lines 10-12 - and that population is the one this arm inherited from the retired /knockoutScheduleHFutaSectionB when Section B stopped being a scope gap. The direction is the retired refusal's own: Section A produces the LOWEST FUTA figure the schedule can, so an unanswered routing question must never default into it.
WHAT ARM 2 IS PROTECTING AGAINST, concretely, is a $0 FUTA tax with nothing refusing it. On the Section A route /scheduleHLine15 is complete-safe to zero and line 16 is 0.6% of zero; on the Section B route an empty employee list zeroes lines 20, 21 and 22 and therefore line 24; on the unanswered-lines-10-12 route neither section computes at all. In each case arm 1 is silent (lines A and B are both No on the line-C route). The intake the first two clauses name is /householdEmployees rather than the retired line 15 attestation, and the predicate tests it with /scheduleHHouseholdEmployeesListed - which is deliberately weaker than the Part I test, because Part II has no per-employee floor.
THE ROW-LEVEL CLAUSES REFUSE ONLY THE UNDER-STATING OMISSIONS, which is the module's standing policy rather than a shortcut. A missing column (a) could hide a credit reduction jurisdiction and a missing Worksheet 2 wage figure on a CA or VI row zeroes the reduction - both inflate the credit and cut the tax. A missing column (b), column (h) or experience rate all shrink the credit and RAISE the tax, so none of them is refused; the reasoning is recorded on /scheduleHFutaStateContributions/*/rowIsIncomplete.
A DATA-COMPLETENESS GUARD, NOT A SCOPE REFUSAL. Nothing here is beyond this module's scope; the filer has simply not finished the schedule. Every Schedule H entry is complete-safe to zero - which is what makes the module additive - so a missing answer would otherwise become an UNDER-stated tax rather than a visible gap. It carries BlockSubmissionOnTrue and is a member of flow /flowIsKnockedOut, as every refusal is; its sidecar revisit trigger is recorded as n/a because nothing here is waiting to be built.
ADDITIVE ON THE COMMITTED CORPUS: no scenario answers line A, line B or the $1,000-quarter question, so neither arm can fire and this resolves Complete false on every committed case.

Fact.Name: Refusal for a filer with a household-employee care provider who has not answered Schedule H
Fact.Description:
Refuses the return whose Form 2441 line 1 column (d) says a care provider IS a household employee (cdcc:/flowKnockoutHouseholdEmployee, derived from the per-provider attestations) while the Schedule H line A / B / C chain has not been walked (/scheduleHGateIsComplete).
THIS IS THE OTHER HALF OF THE HOUSEHOLD-EMPLOYEE KNOCKOUT RETIREMENT, and it is why that retirement is safe. Before this unit, any household employee refused the return outright. After it, Schedule H computes - but every Schedule H intake is complete-safe to zero, so a filer with a household employee whose intake never asks line A would file $0 of household employment tax. The graph holds exactly one signal that such an employee exists, the Form 2441 column (d) attestation, and this refusal spends it: a return that has said "yes, a household employee" and has not settled the Schedule H gate cannot file. "If the care provider is your household employee, you may owe employment taxes. For details, see the Instructions for Schedule H (Form 1040)" (https://www.irs.gov/pub/irs-pdf/f2441.pdf, page 1).
DECLARED GAP, STATED RATHER THAN IMPLIED. Column (d) sees CARE PROVIDERS only. A filer whose household employee is a maid, a yard worker or a private nurse - all named in the instruction's own list of household work (https://www.irs.gov/pub/irs-pdf/i1040sh.pdf, page 2) - is not visible here at all. For them the question genuinely moves to Schedule H line A, which is the right home for it (the old cdcc writable was a dependent-care-flow question standing in for an employment-tax one), and the residual risk is that no intake asks line A: such a return files $0 of household employment tax. That is the SAME $0 it files today, because the old refusal likewise only fires on a question no intake asks - every one of the 697 committed scenarios answers it false - so this unit does not widen the exposure. It is recorded here as the module's principal residual, closed by a SERVICE-side intake for line A (invariant #7).
A DATA-COMPLETENESS GUARD, like its sibling: BlockSubmissionOnTrue with no flow membership, n/a revisit trigger.
ADDITIVE ON THE COMMITTED CORPUS: no care provider in any committed scenario answers /cdccCareProviders/*/writableIsHouseholdEmployee, so cdcc:/flowKnockoutHouseholdEmployee is false on every committed case and this resolves Complete false.
